Overview The Flame Design experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which the tests were conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Richard L. Axelbaum of the Washington University of St. Louis’s Dept. of Energy, Environmental & Chemical Engineering. The Co-Investigator (Co-I) is Prof. Peter B. Sunderland of the University of Maryland’s Dept. of Fire Protection Engineering. The ISS research also benefitted greatly from the work of Phillip H. Irace who was a doctoral student at the Washington University of St. Louis throughout the on-orbit operations. Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME including Flame Design and the rest of the ACME investigations. In ACME’s preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist. For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team included Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam who are also with CWRU. The ISS operations for Flame Design were conducted in two rounds of testing which occurred in April-July 2019 and Oct. 2021 to Feb. 2022. The two rounds occurred during Increments 59/60 and 66 and respectively featured normal and inverse flames. The inverse flame tests were conducted with the chamber filled with a mixture of nitrogen and ethylene

The approach is termed flame design, as it takes a fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed, designs flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. Flame design involves affecting the basic structure of the flame in that the relationship between the temperature and concentration fields is varied to accomplish a stated objective. The method involves exchanging nitrogen (or any inert, including carbon dioxide) from the oxidizer stream to the fuel stream such that the stoichiometric mixture fraction, Zst, can be varied with or without affecting adiabatic flame temperature, Tad. The structure of a high Zst flame is substantially different from that of the standard hydrocarbon/air flame, where Zst is relatively low. By varying Zst at constant Tad, flames have been produced that are soot-free at any strain rate (permanently blue) and have extinction scalar dissipation rates up to 40 times those of their fuel-air counterparts. The nitrogen exchange approach (or some variant of it) has been the subject of many studies by the PI and Co-Is (Du and Axelbaum, 1995, 1996, Chao et al., 1998, Sunderland et al., 2003, 2004, Liu et al., 2005, Chen and Axelbaum, 2005, Kumfer et al., 2006, 2008, Santa et al., 2007a, 2007b, Skeen et al., 2009) and other investigators (Sung et al., 1995; Lin and Faeth, 1996; Kang et al., 1997; Hwang and Chung, 2001). Although these studies have been informative, they typically involved normal-gravity flames, where buoyancy and inherent

It is not known whether this phenomenon is due more to a change in the direction of convection across the flame or to a change in the detailed structure of the flame. This issue can be addressed by performing microgravity experiments because the unique character of nonbuoyant microgravity flames allows the effects of convection direction and flame structure to be independently varied. By ejecting fuel into an oxidizer in a buoyancy free system, the convective flow across the flame is unambiguously from fuel to oxidizer. Alternatively, by ejecting oxidizer into fuel, the flow is from oxidizer to fuel. Furthermore, the long residence times that can be obtained in the spherical flame geometry will allow for validation of a theory that predicts the sooting limits at the limit of infinite Damköhler number, Da. Studies of the effect of Zst on scalar dissipation rate at extinction have indicated that there is a unique Zst where the flame is most resistant to extinction. These findings also suggest that by employing inert exchange to vary Zst, the peak temperature can be shifted to coincide with the location of radical production, thus allowing the flame to burn at much lower temperatures. The optimum minimum temperature at extinction has led us to propose the concept of a pseudo- flammability limit for nonpremixed flames. text: ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 5 will support the experimental investigation. Models will include gas-phase and burner-surface radiation. Specifically, soot-inception limits in spherical flames will be measured by establishing a flame at a given Zst and allowing peak temperature to decrease with time until the yellow luminosity is eliminated. The effect of flow direction across the flame will be studied by performing coflow experiments (desired) where the fuel issues into the oxidizer and oxidizer issues into fuel. Gas temperatures will be measured by thin film pyrometry and thermocouples to identify the soot- inception temperature. In addition, soot volume fraction measurements will be made to evaluate the effects of Zst and flow direction on soot formation and growth, and to better understand the phenomena of permanently-blue flames. Flame extinction limits will also be studied in a manner similar to that of soot inception limits, and temperatures near extinction will be measured. The experiments and modeling will yield unique data that will allow for an understanding of how Zst affects soot-inception and flame extinction and how Zst can be used to design optimum flames. In addition, the effects of flow direction will also be studied and the importance of flow direction and flame structure to permanently-blue flames will be assessed. Finally, the proposed concept of a pseudo-flammability limit for nonpremixed flames will be evaluated and these limits will be ascertained for the test fuels. These results will be useful for the development of future combustion

Previous ground-based microgravity experiments have demonstrated the value of the spherical, burner-supported nonpremixed flames for flame studies. The one-dimensional flame offers a simple, fundamental configuration to improve our understanding of nonpremixed flame behavior and to explore such effects as radiation and thermophoresis, which are more pronounced under microgravity conditions (Atreya et al., 1992, Law et al., 2001). The burner-supported spherical flame is in some respects similar to droplet burning but it holds the advantages that larger flames are possible and, with sufficiently long time, can approach quasi-steady state. Although the spherically-symmetric flame geometry has many advantages, it is not practical to produce such a flame at normal gravity. (2.1) Here g is the acceleration of gravity, T is temperature, L is the characteristic length scale, and u burner surface, and ΔΤ = (Tad – Tb), we find that Ri is on the order of 1000 in normal gravity. In fact, it is much higher than this because the more appropriate length and velocity scales are the flame diameter and the velocity at the flame, respectively. The value of Ri can be reduced by judicious choice of fuels and inert; Law et al. (2001) have shown that nearly spherical flames can be created in normal gravity. However, Ri for these flames is still on the order of unity, implying that while the flames appear spherical, natural convection is still present. Furthermore, hydrogen must be used as a fuel and be supplied in the ambient so such flames are not relevant to this study. A reduction in Ri can be achieved by reducing the flame size, but substantial reduction in L is not practical because our goal is to produce a flame that is sufficiently large that its structure can be characterized. Furthermore, heat loss to the burner would be excessive for small flames. Consequently, for general fuels and inerts the only practical method of obtaining Ri << 1 is to reduce g by four orders of magnitude. This can be accomplished in a number of microgravity environments, including ground-based facilities, e.g., drop towers for short times, as well as flight experiments, e.g., the International Space Station for longer times. The ability to reverse flow direction has helped to elucidate the dominant mechanism responsible for permanently-blue flames, yet the results are not conclusive because transient effects could dominate these observations. Transient effects arise from two sources: the ignition process and the long times required for spherical microgravity flames to reach quasi-steady state. The ignition process is not spherically symmetric and thus there is an asymmetry imposed by ignition that must be damped out. More importantly, soot particles that are created during ignition can be trapped in the interior of the flame due to thermophoresis. The particles are trapped for the same reasons that a soot shell is produced in microgravity droplet combustion (Choi et al., 1991, Avedisian and Callahan, 2000). Thus, it is possible for soot to exist in flames after the ignition event even though the flame has ceased producing soot. To provide a quantitative assessment of the acceptable gravity level, an analysis was performed, as detailed in Appendix A. In this analysis, the acceleration induced on a fluid packet by natural convection is formulated by considering a gravitational acceleration given by a sinusoidal function. The resulting acceleration function for the fluid packet is next integrated to obtain the gravity induced flow velocity. This velocity can be converted to an additional mass flux that transports the flame front and causes distortion of the flame. By specifying the maximum percentage of distortion allowed in the experiment (10% here), the acceptable gravity level is determined, and this result is given in Fig. 2.1 for the four flames of Table 1.1. As shown, the required g levels are on the order of 10 μg. This is too for microgravity aircraft, but is consistent with the anticipated environment of the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). Finally, it is important to emphasize that the proposed experiments illustrate an important and novel use of microgravity for combustion research. In microgravity we are able to hold Zst fixed and in coflow tests vary the direction of convection through the flame. There are no analogous experiments at 1g that can accomplish this. Experiments have been performed in normal gravity coflow flames to understand the effects of flame

As mentioned previously, owing to the effects of buoyancy on the flow field, the flow direction cannot be prescribed in normal gravity coflow flames as it can in microgravity spherical flames or microgravity coflow flames. For example, it is well known that for fuel issuing into an ambient of air, buoyancy accelerates the flow field and causes the streamlines to be from oxidizer to fuel in the lower regions of the flame and from fuel to oxidizer in the upper regions (Santoro et al., 1987). The importance of buoyancy to the flow field will vary with Zst because the velocity and thus Ri are strongly affected by dilution. In other words, the relative amount of entrainment will vary with Zst in buoyant flames. Thus, normal gravity flames have ambiguities with respect to flow direction as Zst is varied. Nonetheless, coflow flames have been valuable in confirming the role of Zst on flame structure and the effects of residence time on soot inception (Kumfer et al., 2006, 2008, Skeen et al., 2009). text: ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 10 Figure 2: Design of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) chamber insert that will be used in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on ISS. ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety of burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter. As depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4 to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1 and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and two flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm). Most burners will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux transducers. The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring of the pressure differential across the outlet surface. The igniter will have a crew-exchangeable tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper-motor drive will allow for precise positioning. Figure 3: ACME burner types, including from left to right, gas-jet burners, a co-flow burner, porous spherical burners, and flat porous burners for the BRE experiment. Ultimately, the spherical burners were limited to a single diameter of 6.35 mm, and the fabricated gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 1.3 and 2.1 mm.

text: ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 12 support the operations and provide reference images. The 12-bit digital camera records at up to 30 full frames (1360x1024) per second, and is equipped with a motorized lens with independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus. The digital camera will be equipped with a filter assembly with four options, where selection of a clear “filter” allows for color imaging. Color imaging can also be carried out with a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, which balances the color planes to avoid saturation in the red while maintaining sensitivity in the blue and green. The natural flame color can be approximately reconstructed, but the primary purpose of the filter is pyrometry and measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniques of [23-24]. Alternately, CH* imaging can be conducted with this camera because the filter assembly includes a 430-nm bandpass filter with a 10-nm full width at half-maximum transmission (FWHM). A 450-nm bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively subtract interfering broadband soot emission. Each PMT will have a wide-angle view, a sight line that is orthogonal to the chamber axis, and will be centered (along the chamber length) relative to the chamber windows so that it is aligned with most of the other instrumentation. The PMTs’ spectral range will be 230-700 nm, i.e., visible and near ultraviolet, but one will have a 310-nm bandpass filter and another will have a 430-nm bandpass filter (where both are with a 10-nm FWHM). Like many other components, the PMT array can be removed from the chamber insert by the crew. Unlike the radiometers, each PMT had a readily adjustable gain. The chamber insert is also equipped with six far-field thermocouples to measure the spread of the thermal field in the spherical flame experiments. They are of limited utility for other experiments because they are positioned upstream of the burner tip. Summary of Preliminary Results Abstract for Critical temperature and reactant mass flux for radiative extinction of ethylene microgravity spherical diffusion flames at 1 bar (2023): In microgravity combustion, where buoyancy is not present to accelerate the flow field and strain the flame, radiative extinction is of fundamental importance, and has implications for spacecraft fire safety. In this work, the critical point for radiative extinction is identified for normal and inverse ethylene spherical diffusion flames via atmospheric pressure experiments conducted aboard the International Space Station, as well as with a transient numerical model. The fuel is ethylene with nitrogen diluent, and the oxidizer is an oxygen/nitrogen mixture. The burner is a porous stainless-steel sphere. All experiments are conducted at constant reactant flow rate. For normal flames, the ambient oxygen mole fraction was varied from 0.2 to 0.38, burner supply fuel mole fraction from 0.13 to 1, total mass flow rate, mtotal , from 0.6 to 12.2 mg/s, and adiabatic flame temperature, Tad , from 2000 to 2800 K. For inverse flames, the ambient fuel mole fraction was varied from 0.08 to 0.12, burner supply oxygen mole fraction from 0.4 to 0.85, mtotal from 2.3 to 11.3 mg/s, and Tad from 2080 to 2590 K. Despite this broad range of conditions, all flames extinguish at a critical extinction temperature of 1130 K, and a fuel-based mass flux of 0.2 g/m2 - s for normal flames, and an oxygen- based mass flux of 0.68 g/m2-s for inverse flames. Experimental results are compared with a transient numerical model. The experiments involve normal spherical diffusion flames (i.e., fuel flowing into oxidizer) burning ethylene in an oxygen/nitrogen mixture at atmospheric pressure. The stoichiometric mixture fraction and adiabatic flame temperature are varied by diluting the fuel with nitrogen and varying the oxygen concentration in the ambient. The diagnostics consist of color video, thin-filament pyrometry for gas temperature, thermocouple measurements of burner temperature, and photomultiplier tube measurements of broad and narrow-band flame emission. Radiative extinction is observed when, at constant reactant flow rate, the flame expands until radiation heat loss approaches the chemical heat release. Before a flame experiences complete extinction, it may enter an oscillatory mode in which part of the flame partially extinguishes and then reforms. Impacts, Benefits, and Products The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. text: ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 32 Flame Design investigates the soot inception and extinction limits of spherical microgravity flames created with porous spherical burners. Tests are conducted with various concentrations of both the fuel (e.g., ethylene) and oxygen in order to determine the role of the flame structure on the soot inception. More specifically, Flame Design has the following experimental objectives which are listed here in priority order. It must be emphasized that NASA does not currently plan to carry out the desired or highly desired testing with carbon dioxide, pressure as a variable (except to a limited degree), coflow flames, or methane. A. Obtain soot-inception limits of quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames as functions of flow rate, Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2**), and pressure** for C2H4 and CH4* flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Obtain similar limits and temperatures for inverse and normal coflow flames**. B. Obtain detailed measurements in quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames for C2H4 and CH4*. Determine the effects of flow rate, Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2**), and pressure** on flame temperature, size, color, and soot volume fraction. Evaluate the possible existence of steady flames. Obtain similar measurements for inverse and normal coflow flames**. C. Obtain extinction limits as functions of Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2**), and pressure** for normal and inverse spherical C2H4 and CH4 * flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions.

text: studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the flicker of flame, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. Flame Design should yield unique data that allows for a better understanding of how nitrogen exchange affects soot-inception and flame extinction, and how it can be used to design optimum flames. In addition, the effects of flow direction are also studied, and the importance of the flow direction and flame structure to permanently-blue flames is assessed.

Discussion of Method/Protocol Flame Design and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it may alternately be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. For example, the flow rate can be adjusted to approach a flame’s soot limit. This was not done during Increments 59 and 60, where the console commanding during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed in the analog ops video that the flame had extinguished. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing. III. Results A. All of the raw (hobj) images obtained from the ACME camera have been successfully converted to tiff files for further analysis. Thin filament pyrometry is being used to obtain fiber temperature measurements in ACME camera images that have SiC fibers inserted in the flame. Soot temperature measurements using two-color ratio pyrometry are being acquired from ACME camera images that have soot and no fibers. text: flames in microgravity have unique characteristics that are valuable for fundamental studies of diffusion flames. Flame size increases with reactant flow rate and decreases with ambient oxygen concentration. Radiative heat loss scales with flame size such that very small flames - just above their kinetic extinction limits - have low radiative loss, and asymptotically approach steady-state behavior. Larger flames increase in size over time until the rate of radiative heat loss exceeds the rate of chemical heat release, and the flame extinguishes via radiative extinction. Before total extinction occurs in these flames, they experience an unstable, oscillatory mode, in which they partially extinguish and reform. The oscillations grow in magnitude until total extinction. For constant ambient oxygen concentration, larger flames (with higher fuel flow rates) radiatively extinguish faster than smaller flames (with lower flow rates) due to higher radiative losses and decreasing chemical heat release. Small, asymptotically quasi-steady flames are found to have low radiative losses and nearly constant chemical heat release. A thorough analysis of low flow rate flames was completed in order to investigate the existence of steady-state spherical flames, which has been a subject of debate in literature. This analysis is described in the submission to the 38th International Symposium on Combustion cited below. 1. P. Irace, H. Lee, K. Waddell, L. Tan, D. Stocker, D. Urban, P. Sunderland, and R. Axelbaum, “Steady-state burner stabilized spherical diffusion flames in microgravity,” 38th International

text: ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 40 The abstract from this submission states: This study is an examination of steady-state behavior in spherical diffusion flames in microgravity on the International Space Station (ISS). Gaseous spherical diffusion flames stabilized on a porous sphere were employed in a normal configuration (i.e., fuel issuing into an ambient oxidizer). The use of a porous sphere allowed for a spherical flame with a constant mass flow rate, a condition that is not attainable with free-droplet combustion. Unlike previous microgravity spherical flame studies, time is not a limitation for these experiments, and the potential to achieve steady-state flames can be explored for the first time. Stoichiometric mixture fraction, Zst, and flame temperature were varied by diluting the fuel with nitrogen, or changing the ambient oxygen concentration, either 21 or 40 vol% oxygen. Flame size was found to increase with increasing fuel flow rate and decrease with increasing ambient oxygen concentration. The large spherical diffusion flames were observed to grow until extinction, while small flames were found to exhibit an asymptotically steady behavior due to their low radiative losses and faster transport. Experimental measurements of flame size were in quantitative agreement with numerical results with one-step chemistry, provided the diffusivity was appropriately adjusted. Alternatively, by ejecting oxidizer from the burner into an atmosphere of fuel, the flow is from oxidizer to fuel. Furthermore, microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the flicker of flame, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. Flame Design should yield unique data that allows for a better understanding of how nitrogen exchange affects soot-inception and flame extinction,

text: ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 45 II. Methods/Research Operations B. Discussion of Method/Protocol Flame Design and other ACME experiments were configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role was to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes included the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All ACME testing was commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of ACME testing was conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. While it was possible to make some ‘manual’ changes outside of the script, e.g., to approach a flame’s soot limit, during a test that was not done in any ACME testing, neglecting minor exceptions, e.g., to terminate tests after the flames had extinguished. Testing was not conducted when thrusters fired or spacecraft docked or undocked from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data was downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing. III. Results G. The ACME camera is not of sufficient quality to demonstrate the novel aspects of the experiments to the public, but it appears to have been satisfactory from a science perspective. Regardless of the shortcomings discussed above, a great wealth of experimental data has been secured and Flame Design’s first round is considered to be at least minimally successful despite the imperfect symmetry. text: with reactant flow rate and decreases with ambient oxygen concentration. Radiative heat loss scales with flame size such that very small flames - just above their kinetic extinction limits - have low radiative loss, and asymptotically approach steady-state behavior. Larger flames increase in size over time until the rate of radiative heat loss becomes sufficiently large, and the flame extinguishes via radiative extinction. Before total extinction occurs in these flames, they experience an unstable, oscillatory mode, in which they partially extinguish and reform. The oscillations grow in magnitude until total extinction. For constant ambient oxygen concentration, larger flames (with higher fuel flow rates) radiatively extinguish faster than smaller flames (with lower flow rates) due to higher radiative losses and decreasing chemical heat release. A thorough analysis of low flow rate flames was completed in order to investigate the existence of steady-state spherical flames, which has been a subject of debate in literature. It was found that steady state microgravity spherical diffusion flames can exist. Furthermore, it was found that ethylene microgravity spherical diffusion flames at 1 bar extinguish at a critical extinction point defined by an extinction flame temperature and an extinction reactant mass flux at the flame. These analyses are described in the manuscripts accepted for the 39th International Symposium on Combustion cited below.

Axelbaum, On the existence of steady state gaseous microgravity spherical diffusion flames in the presence of radiation heat loss, Proceedings of the Combustion Institute 2022 (accepted). The abstract from this submission states: Whether steady-state gaseous microgravity spherical diffusion exist in the presence of radiation heat loss is an important fundamental question and has important implications for spacecraft fire safety. In this work, experiments aboard the International Space Station and a transient numerical model are used to investigate the existence of steady-state microgravity spherical diffusion flames. Gaseous spherical diffusion flames stabilized on a porous spherical burner are employed in normal (i.e., fuel flowing into an ambient oxidizer) and inverse (i.e., oxidizer flowing into an ambient fuel) flame configurations. The fuel is ethylene and the oxidizer oxygen, both diluted with nitrogen. The flow rate of the reactant gas from the burner is held constant. It is found that steady-state gaseous microgravity spherical diffusion flames do exist in the presence of radiation heat loss, provided that the steady-state flame size is less than the flame size for radiative extinction, and the flame develops fast enough that radiation heat loss does not drop the flame temperature below the critical temperature for radiative extinction (1130 K). A simple model is provided that allows for the identification of initial conditions

text: ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 58 Appendix F. ISS Operations per the Payload Weekly Science Summary 2019 First round (normal flames) Increment 59/60 Week 5: April 5-11 This week, Christina Koch configured the ACME Chamber Insert to support the next ACME experiment, Flame Design. Also to support Flame Design, Oleg Kononenko replaced the bottles on CIR Manifold #2, CIR Manifold #4, and the CIR GC Helium Manifold. Flame Design is focused on understanding the soot processes of flames. Test points will start in a few weeks. The April 11 reporting on the completion of BRE’s first round was not included here. Week 8: April 26 – May 2 On GMT 115, the first ACME Flame Design test points were performed. Pure gaseous ethylene fuel was ejected into air from a porous sphere, which, in microgravity, results in a one-dimensional, spherical flame. Thus, data analysis is greatly simplified because the flame shape doesn’t need to be predicted, and computational modeling can focus on the detailed chemistry and transport of the molecules and energy. The goal of Flame Design is to improve our understanding of soot processes so that flames can be “designed” to be soot free. This research could help lead to reduced soot and NOx—and thus reduced smog and acid rain—through nitrogen exchange, where the nitrogen is shifted from the air to the fuel. (a) Shortly after ignition, the ignition-created soot is being carried out of the flame by the gas flow from the porous spherical burner. text: ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 62 Week 14: June 7-13 On GMT 156, ACME Flame Design test conditions resulted in flames which continued to produce soot following ignition, yielding new information for this study of soot processes. While soot is both an environmental and health concern, it can be useful for some applications. As two examples, soot is helpful for radiant heat transfer and for illumination. The purpose of Flame Design is to determine the conditions controlling the presence or absence of soot in non-premixed flames (i.e., where the fuel and oxygen are separated by the flame’s surface). With that understanding, engineers will be able to “design” flames that are either sooty or not depending on their needs. At ignition, the flame is very sooty. The broadband thermal radiation of the soot particles causes the bright yellow color of the flame. The test conditions are such that the flame temperature is high enough to continue to produce soot particles, which are mostly carbon and form when the ethylene within the flame is hot enough to react with itself in the absence of oxygen (which is outside of the flame). text: ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 63 While Flame Design’s primary objective is to determine the conditions under which flames are soot-free or soot producing, a secondary objective is to establish flammability limits for these spherical flames. We have observed interesting phenomena where the flames sometimes self-extinguish after growing oscillations. These oscillations are apparent in the above graph, which shows the chemiluminescence from excited molecules that drop to a lower energy state by emitting a photon at a specific wavelength. CH* chemiluminescence is the source of most of the blue seen in hydrocarbon flames and OH* chemiluminescence is in the ultraviolet. These two measurements are made with Photomultipiler Tubes (PMTs), where each tube is equipped with a narrow-band filter corresponding to an excited molecule. In the example shown in the graph, the flame’s oscillations lasted about 30 seconds and occurred at roughly 1 Hz, but they slowed in frequency as they grew in strength. The oscillations are evident in the imaging, where the flame locally quenches—creating a hole in the flame. This hole allows for increased mixing of the fuel and oxygen, which in turn results in a recovery of the flame. The size of the opening in the flame (which normally separates the fuel and oxygen) grows with time until the entire flame extinguishes. Interestingly, the graph shows that the CH* measurement was relatively steady before the start of the oscillations in comparison with the decaying OH* emission. This difference will be further examined to improve our understanding

While the temperature measurements are being made, the flow of diluted ethylene is gradually reduced, which causes the flame to become smaller and unstable. Heat loss causes the flame to locally quench—creating a hole in the flame near the burner tube. This hole allows for increased mixing of the fuel and oxygen, which reinvigorates the flame and causes it to close again. The flame opens and closes, effectively consuming fuel in repeated gulps…a bit like a video-game character eating dots. But as the fuel flow is reduced further, the size of the open “mouth” gets smaller, as if the flame is becoming full. The flame becomes stable again until the flow becomes so small that the flame finally goes out. This video illustrates the extreme complexities of even conceptually simple flames! Even though mankind has been using combustion for millennia, microgravity research can unlock new understanding, which would lead to improved efficiency and reduced pollutant emission in practical terrestrial combustion.

text: ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 67 Week 7: Nov. 26 – Dec. 2 On GMT 328, we ignited nine inverse flames for ACME Flame Design. For these tests, an oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowed from the burner into a combustion chamber, which was filled with an ethylene/nitrogen mixture. For one of these tests, we observed our longest sustained flame, which burned for over 14 minutes. At that time, operational constraints required its termination. For comparison, flame durations for all ACME experiments are typically shorter than two minutes with the longest—until now—under six minutes. This 14+ minute flame has led to new understanding of the stability of spherical flames. While test measurements did show that this long-duration flame was slowly weakening with time, it might have burned significantly longer. We have found with higher burner flow rates that flames grow with time and extinguish due to radiative heat loss. If the flow rate is too low, the flame’s small size leads to excessive burner heating. But under the right conditions, the flame can burn for minutes and perhaps even tens of minutes. Figure 1. text: ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 93 Appendix M. Summary of the ISS data collection The Flame Design data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where that is generally true for the ACME experiments. To be clear, there was no collection of soot or other physical samples that were subsequently transported to the ground. The Flame Design image data includes images from the following cameras: 1. ACME DataCam, used with a clear fused-silica ‘filter’ and various zoom and focus settings (but those settings were consistent within each individual test) 2. CFI intensified camera, used at least generally with a CH* filter 3. High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a red filter corresponding to the opposing CIR illumination package The raw DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic Object (hobj) format as well as a converted Tagged Image File (tif) format. NASA’s post-processing of the raw images was carried out without each of the following: a. color balancing (to avoid possible saturation) b. dark frame subtraction c. removal of hot spots from dead pixels (e.g., resulting from radiation damage) Furthermore, the conversion employed a standard bilinear demosaicing process which is detrimental when determining temperature profiles via Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) because it will average pixels both on and off the glowing fibers. The images from the CFI and HiBMs cameras are provided in a tif format. Meanwhile, the analog operations (ops) video was recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. text: Task Description: NOTE Update August 2020: New grant issued for Flame Design - A Novel Approach to Clean Efficient Diffusion Flames, with grant number 80NSSC20M0072, which continues to 4/30/2022. NOTE (September 2015): Continuation of Flame Design - A Novel Approach to Clean Efficient Diffusion Flames (NNX09AO53A). The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. This effort is a collaborative effort between the PI (Principal Investigator), the Co-Is (Co-Investigators), and staff at NASA Glenn Research Center. The division of labor has Richard Axelbaum directing normal gravity experiments and computations at Washington University, David Urban providing guidance for the flight experiments, and Peter Sunderland

Rationale for HRP Directed Research: Research Impact/Earth Benefits: This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors. For example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants. Task Progress: We have completed Round 1 (normal flames) and Round 2 (inverse flames) of Flame Design testing and are processing and analyzing the data. We are running Sphdif simulations and publishing the findings. Three journal papers were published this year and one other was submitted. One conference paper was published and presented. Kendyl Waddell defended and published his Ph.D. dissertation. Our work on the numerical model has continued. We have run multiple cases with the University of California San Diego (UCSD) mechanism. We continue to investigate the boundary conditions for radiation and conduction. We simulated ethylene flames to perform parametric studies in an attempt to find conditions that are favorable to steady state flames. February 2024 Update per PI. See Bibliography for additional information. (Ed., 2/15/24) Despite a range of conditions, all flames extinguish at a critical temperature of 1130 K, a fuel-based mass flux of 0.2 g/m2-s for normal flames, and an oxygen-based mass flux of 0.68 g/m2-s for inverse flames. With this information, we have developed a simple equation to estimate the flame size (i.e., location of peak temperature) at extinction for any atmospheric-pressure ethylene spherical diffusion flame given

text: Task Description: NOTE Update August 2020: New grant issued for Flame Design - A Novel Approach to Clean Efficient Diffusion Flames, with grant number 80NSSC20M0072, which continues to 4/30/2022. NOTE (September 2015): Continuation of Flame Design - A Novel Approach to Clean Efficient Diffusion Flames (NNX09AO53A). The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. This effort is a collaborative effort between the PI (Principal Investigator), the Co-Is (Co-Investigators), and staff at NASA Glenn Research Center. The division of labor has Richard Axelbaum directing normal gravity experiments and computations at Washington University, David Urban providing guidance for the flight experiments, and Peter Sunderland

text: of radiant emissions in ethylene tri-axial flames. Soot volume fraction measurements using color pyrometry and an absolute intensity calibration have been performed. In our research on double luminous zones, we have made our chemiluminescence images quantitative and have chosen some of them to be displayed as color contour plots of intensity at specific wavelengths. Thermocouple probing of the double luminous zones was performed. Work continued on the imaging of excited species. An analytical model of steady-state diameters of gas-fed spherical diffusion flames was created. Our work on the numerical model has continued. We have run multiple cases with the University of California San Diego (UCSD) mechanism. We continue to investigate the boundary conditions for radiation and conduction. Because burner heating can significantly affect the flame diameter and lifetime, we have started to implement a heat balance at the burner surface to solve for burner temperature and better conserve enthalpy. Scientific Context, Hypothesis, and Research Objectives: The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. text: At Washington University in the last two months, we have performed experiments to show the PM emissions from the pure ethylene flame and comparing PM (particulate matter) data of newly bought low pressure impactor [Electrical Low-Pressure Impactor (ELPI), model ELPI+, Dekati] and Scanning Mobility Particle Spectrometry (SMPS, model 3080, TSI Inc.). A rich ethylene flame was chosen as it produces soot at a uniform rate. A co-flow diffusion flame burner was used, which comprised of two coaxial channels for the flow of fuel and air, respectively. Particle sampling is achieved with an N2-diluted sampling probe. The flow of dilution N2 through the annulus gap provides the negative pressure needed to sample the flue gas as well as cool down and dilute the particle-laden flow. The dilution ratio (DR) is controlled by N2 flow rate and the physical dimension of the annulus gap, and CO2 is chosen as the tracer gas for dilution ratio measurement. A high flow rate of dilution N2 (~45 SLPM) is applied and the dilution ratio is controlled to a range of 30 – 200. The probe samples the whole particle stream while maintaining quasi-isokinetic sampling, and is expected to cause little bias for particle measurements. The ELPI and SMPS (scanning mobility particle spectrometer) data show similar trends. The experiments were also conducted to know the efficiency of ELPI with respect to time to get the correct PSD (particle size distribution) data. It was found that after 2 minutes of measurements, ELPI have to be cleaned as it creates a virtual mode owing to the partly over filing of ELPI stages.

text: Based on recent findings, the new graduate student at Washington University is beginning to construct a tri-coflow burner to test a theory of applying Flame Design concepts to control heat flux. We have modified an existing burner to create a triaxial coflow flame. The inner nozzle supplies air or oxygen enriched air, the middle nozzle supplies fuel (methane) or nitrogen diluted fuel, and the outer nozzle supplies air or oxygen enriched air. The inner oxidizer creates an inner flame sheet, resulting in two distinct flame zones. The goal of this project is to maximize radiation heat transfer in methane combustion by using flame design concepts to create a soot favorable environment at the inner flame sheet and then oxidize soot particles before they are released to the ambient environment. We have been taking high speed videos of the flame sheet interactions and are preparing to take radiation measurements. text: Task Description: NOTE: Continuation of Flame Design - A Novel Approach to Clean Efficient Diffusion Flames (NNX09AO53A). The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. This effort is a collaborative effort between the PI (Principal Investigator), the Co-Is (Co-Investigators), and staff at NASA Glenn Research Center. The division of labor has Richard Axelbaum directing normal gravity experiments and computations at Washington University, David Urban providing guidance for the flight experiments, and Peter Sunderland directing experiments and numerical simulations at University of Maryland. Task Progress: The laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) measurement method has been improved at Washington University in St. Louis. This includes a new oscilloscope setup and preparation for better acoustic monitoring. We have synchronized the new oscilloscope with the LIBS system. We completed work on noise filtering of the acoustic measurements. We performed Matlab programming on automated acoustic aided LIBS measurements. We performed high temperature LIBS tests in a Hencken burner, LIBS tests in a McKenna burner under same equivalence ratio and different temperature, and acoustic aided LIBS measurements in a McKenna burner with varying equivalence ratio. We adapted a maximum likelihood estimation method instead of average in LIBS data processing; compared and correlated the baseline for different element emission lines; and worked on the scalar measurement. We investigated the compositional effects in laser-induced backward transfer (LIBT) measurement and investigated the screening methods of LIBT measurement by looking into the statistics. We investigated the simultaneous composition and temperature measurement using laser induced plasma. We explored the water-gas-shift equilibrium in higher hydrocarbon flames and investigated the potential of inferring molecular profiles from LIBS measured elemental compositions. We investigated the water-gas-shift equilibrium in higher hydrocarbons using detailed mechanisms for heptane and toluene.

text: We developed a plasma model to simulate the sound wave generation as a function of laser energy input and local gas properties and to optimize the measurements using a CCD based spectrometer. Wendong Wu successfully defended his Ph.D. in May, 2017, at Washington University in St. Louis. The collaboration between Washington University and Shanghai Jiaotong University will continue in the field of laser plasma diagnostics. Graduate student Pan Du has joined the Flame Design team. At the University of Maryland, we continue to examine the effects of dilution on lengths of normal and inverse gas jet diffusion flames. The method of measuring flame lengths was refined to examine only the blue intensities in the recorded images. Both normal and inverse flames now correlate together according to the theory of Roper. We have also characterized the double flame structure visible in some inverse diffusion flames. We imaged the double flames at 310 and 430 nm. Scientific Context, Hypothesis, and Research Objectives The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. This effort is a collaborative effort between the PI, the three Co-Is, and staff at NASA Glenn Research Center. The kinetic behavior of the water-gas-shift (WGS) sub-system has been studied computationally for hydrocarbon diffusion flames in the counterflow geometry. Of specific interest was the spatial domain in which the reactions in the WGS-complex exhibit characteristics that lead to species concentrations approaching those expected from equilibrium. Two scenarios were observed for WGS equilibrium: (1) Full equilibrium in which every step of the WGS-mechanism is nearly in equilibrium; (2) “Apparent” equilibrium, which is achieved via opposing but coherent shifts away from equilibrium for the two key elementary reactions that constitute the WGS reaction. This interesting phenomenon is caused by the supply of the H radical, which participates in the forward reaction of one step and the reverse reaction of the other. This new form of apparent equilibrium differs from well-known “quasi” equilibrium, which is typically caused by the combination of a fast reversible step and slow irreversible step. Parametric domains where found in which these two scenarios are observed. For a given fuel type it was shown that the two scenarios can be separated by the location of stoichiometry. On the oxidizer side, full equilibrium of the overall WGS reaction

The analytical model of Roper (CNF 29:219, 1977) accounts for the full range of reactant dilution and inverse flames, but has only been tested for fuel-air systems. This work examines the stoichiometric lengths of normal and inverse steady methane/oxygen/nitrogen jet flames burning on a 3.0 mm coflowing burner inside a glass chimney. Nitrogen dilution is such that methane mole fractions vary from 0.15 – 1 and oxygen mole fractions vary from 0.18 – 1. The measured flame lengths vary from 3 – 53 mm. Stoichiometric lengths are measured from visible emissions of the blue flame sheets. Reactant flow rates are measured with calibrated rotameters. The predictions of the Roper model are compared with the measured flame lengths. For normal flames the agreement is best for a mass diffusivity at 25 C of 17 mm2/s and a temperature of 0.94 times the adiabatic flame temperature. This contrasts to values used by Roper for methane/air flames of 20 mm2/s and 1500 K, respectively. For the present conditions the predictions match the measurements with a R2 coefficient of determination of 0.91. For fixed fuel flow rate, inert addition to the fuel stream is found to increase flame length, but this effect is negligible for fuel mole fractions above 0.5. A simplified approximation of the Roper model has been obtained for normal methane/nitrogen/oxygen diffusion flames. This removes the requirement to specify adiabatic flame temperature

text: and stoichiometric mixture fraction. The simplified model predicts flame length from the methane flow rate and mole fraction and the oxygen mole fraction. W. Wu, R.L. Axelbaum, Interpreting Flame Structure by Mixture Fraction Measurement Using Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy, Abstract, ASGSR, Cleveland OH (2016). Measuring mixture fractions in a broad range of combustion systems with a suitable spatial and temporal resolution is critical not only for understanding the flame behavior, but also for the validation of rapidly developing numerical models. Instead of deriving the mixture fraction from measured molecular profile, a new approach of obtaining such quantities from atomic ratios measured by laser induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) is introduced in this study. The atomic ratios for C, N, H, and O (e.g., C/O, H/O, and N/O) for the LIBS system were first calibrated in an ethylene-air premixed flat flame, where the equivalence ratio of the pre-mixture was varied from 0.60 to 1.80. Then the atomic ratio distributions along the centerline of an ethylene-air counter-flow diffusion flame were measured to demonstrate the capability of LIBS to measure atomic ratios between different elements throughout the entire flame. The elemental mass fractions for C, H, N, O can be thus obtained from atomic ratio profiles. The mixture fraction distribution was calculated from elemental mass fractions. Numerical results were compared to the experimental results and showed excellent agreement. The results of this work demonstrate that the LIBS technique holds promise as a simple tool

Axelbaum, Recent Advances in Flame Design, A Spaceflight Combustion Experiment, Abstract, ASGSR, Alexandria, VA, 2015. Flame Design is a spaceflight combustion experiment that will examine several unusual aspects of spherical diffusion flames fueled by gases. Its emphasis is on soot formation and flame extinction. This experiment, and associated ground-based work, attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. This presentation will introduce the overall concepts of Flame Design. It will summarize observations in the NASA Glenn 2.2 s and 5 s drop facilities, which have yielded important insights into soot formation and flame extinction behavior. Detailed numerical modeling of spherical diffusion flames have aided the understanding of the observations. Recent advances in Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy (LIBS) will be discussed. LIBS allows the C/O atom ratio to be measured in flames. This diagnostic is well suited to use in spaceflight experiments. text: Task Description: The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. text: were heavily diluted with water and sprayed into a swirl-stabilized burner and the blow-off limits were obtained to identify the flame stability. The blow-off limit was experimentally determined as the lowest O2 concentration where a flame could exist under a given oxidizer flow rate. For the present experimental system, stability maps were determined as a function of fuel concentration and oxidizer flow rate for different types of nozzles and both alcohols. Contours of temperature and overall fuel mass fraction in the droplets were obtained for a flame burning 15 wt% ethanol in an oxidizer of 50% O2 and 50% N2. The results revealed that preferential vaporization of ethanol over water plays an important role in enhancing flame stability. To further understand this, a model of bi-component droplet vaporization was employed for both the diffusion limit and distillation limit modes of liquid mass transfer. The results confirmed the preferential vaporization of ethanol and demonstrated that it is necessary to account for the non-ideal solution behavior of the alcohol-water mixture to appropriately model the vaporization process. The model also demonstrated that for this experimental system, droplet vaporization was better characterized by the distillation limit mode with enhanced mass transfer by convection. The corresponding author for this paper was R.L. Axelbaum. NOTE (Ed., 7/23/2014): This project is being continued as a new grant to be awarded in fall 2014. See that task for subsequent reporting. text: Task Description: The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. This effort is a collaborative effort between the PI, the three Co-Is, and staff at NASA Glenn Research Center. The division of labor has PBS and DLU performing microgravity experiments at the NASA Glenn Research Center, PBS directing numerical simulations at University of Maryland, BHC performing analytical work and computations at University of Hawaii, and RLA performing normal gravity experiments and computations at Washington University. text: Task Description: The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. This effort is a collaborative effort between the PI, the three Co-Is, and staff at NASA Glenn Research Center. The division of labor is roughly broken up with PBS and DLU performing microgravity experiments at the NASA Glenn Research Center, PBS directing numerical simulations at University of Maryland, BHC performing analytical work and computations at University of Hawaii, and RLA performing normal gravity experiments and computations at Washington University. Rationale for HRP Directed Research: Research Impact/Earth Benefits: This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors.

text: gas Lewis number would have a strong effect on flame temperature if the flames were steady and nonradiating. For example, a 10% decrease in Lewis number would increase the steady state flame temperature by 200 K. However, for these transient, radiating flames the effect of Lewis number is small. It was also observed that when hydrocarbon fuel is supplied from the ambient the large diffusion distances associated with these flames can lead to unusual steady state compositions near the outer boundary because decomposition products can diffuse to the outer boundary. This results in a loss of chemical enthalpy from the system but the effect on flame temperature is small. Transient predictions of flame sizes are larger than those observed in microgravity experiments. Close agreement could not be obtained without either increasing the model’s thermal and mass diffusion properties by 30% or reducing mass flowrate by 25%. 2) Radiative Extinction of Gaseous Spherical Diffusion Flames in Microgravity. Radiative extinction of spherical diffusion flames was investigated experimentally and numerically. The experiments involved microgravity spherical diffusion flames burning ethylene and propane at 0.98 bar. Both normal (fuel flowing into oxidizer) and inverse (oxidizer flowing into fuel) flames were studied, with nitrogen supplied to either the fuel or the oxygen. Flame conditions were chosen to ensure that the flames extinguished within the 2.2 s of available test time; thus extinction occurred during unsteady flame conditions. Diagnostics included color video and thin-filament pyrometry.

Radiative extinction was observed experimentally and simulated numerically. Extinction time, peak temperature, and radiative loss fraction were found to be independent of flow rate except at very low flow rates. Radiative heat loss was dominated by the combustion products downstream of the flame and was found to scale with flame surface area, not volume. For large transient flames the heat release rate also scaled with surface area and thus the radiative loss fraction was largely independent of flow rate. Peak temperatures at extinction onset were about 1100 K, which is significantly lower than for kinetic extinction. text: Zst on soot inception are investigated in normal and inverse coflow flames, using ethylene as the fuel. Use of the inverse coflow flame underscores the validity of these concepts, since the convective field in the inverse flame directs particles into the fuel-rich region. Sooting limits based on particle luminosity are measured as a function of Zst. The sooting limit is obtained by varying the amount of inert gas until soot appears above a predefined height. For each limit flame, the adiabatic flame temperature is calculated and the flame temperature at the half-height is measured. The flame temperature at the sooting limit is found to increase with Zst for both normal and inverse flames. The effects of residence time are also investigated, and the sooting limit inception temperature is found to be dependent on fuel stream velocity for both the normal and inverse configurations. A simple model applicable to oxy–fuel combustion is presented which describes how increasing Zst results in the reduction and ultimately elimination of soot. This model assumes that soot inception can only occur in a region where critical values for species, temperature, and residence time are met. The soot inception region is shown to be bounded by two isotherms: a low-temperature boundary that is a function of residence time, and a high-temperature boundary that corresponds to the location of a critical local carbon-to-oxygen ratio. The effect of increasing Zst is to move the boundaries of the soot inception zone towards each other, until the zone is infinitely thin and thus the sooting limit is reached.

The Presence of Appreciable Oxygen at the Location of Maximum Temperature. The presence of appreciable molecular oxygen at the location of maximum temperature has been observed in non-premixed oxygen-enhanced combustion (OEC) processes, specifically in flames having a high stoichiometric mixture fraction (Zst) produced with diluted fuel and oxygen-enrichment. For conventional fuel–air flames, key features of the flame are consistent with the flame sheet approximation (FSA). In particular, the depletion of O2 at the location of maximum temperature predicted by the FSA correlates well with the near-zero O2 concentration measured at this location for conventional fuel–air flames. text: Task Description: The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed 'Flame Design' as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. Recognizing the unique benefits of spherical diffusion flames, employ such flames to: 1. Obtain soot-inception limits as functions of stoichiometric mixture fraction, flow direction (direction across the flame front, i.e., towards the fuel or towards the oxidizer), amount of inert (nitrogen) and pressure for ethylene and methane flames. Identify the corresponding soot-inception temperature; 2. Determine effects of stoichiometric mixture fraction and flow direction on the phenomenon of permanently blue flames and, to this end, determine the effects of stoichiometric mixture fraction and flow direction on flame temperature, size, color and soot volume

text: Task Description: The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed 'Flame Design' as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. Recognizing the unique benefits of spherical diffusion flames, employ such flames to: 1. Obtain soot-inception limits as functions of stoichiometric mixture fraction, flow direction (direction across the flame front, i.e., towards the fuel or towards the oxidizer), amount of inert (nitrogen) and pressure for ethylene and methane flames. Identify the corresponding soot-inception temperature; 2. Determine effects of stoichiometric mixture fraction and flow direction on the phenomenon of permanently blue flames and, to this end, determine the effects of stoichiometric mixture fraction and flow direction on flame temperature, size, color and soot volume

text: with the present interest in carbon sequestration via oxygen-enriched combustion the present work is of particular importance as it identifies methods of controlling a number of pollutants through oxygen-enriched combustion. Task Progress: Testing in the 2.2-second drop tower has yielded sooting limits of spherical microgravity diffusion flames reacting ethylene and oxygen at various levels of dilution. The results provide a quantitative comparison of the effects on sooting limits of stoichiometric mixture fraction and convection direction. Testing in the drop tower also has identified a number of extinction limits. Normal-gravity tests involving coflowing gas jet flames have considered a similar range of stoichiometric mixture fraction for both normal and inverse conditions. These results lend support to the microgravity observations. Analytical modeling has advanced the understanding of the steady-state temperature, size, and residence times of the present spherical flames. Numerical modeling, which incorporates detailed chemistry and transport, has lent insight into the effects of radiation and unsteadiness of the present spherical flames. These results have been and are being disseminated in the publications listed in the publication section. Normal-gravity tests involving coflowing gas jet flames have considered a similar range of stoichiometric mixture fraction for both normal and inverse conditions. These results lend support to the microgravity observations. Analytical modeling has advanced the understanding of the steady-state temperature, size, and residence times of the present spherical flames. Numerical modeling, which incorporates detailed chemistry and transport, has lent insight into the effects of radiation and unsteadiness of the present spherical flames. These results have been and are being disseminated in the publications listed in the publication section. text: The objectives of the SAFFIRE ( Spacecraft Fire Experiment ) experiments are to (1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test . The specific objective of SAFFIRE-I and SAFFIRE-II I tests is to determine how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low-gravity and whether it reaches a steady-state spread rate. The sample material for SAFFIRE-I and SAFFIRE-III is a composite fabric consisting of cotton on a fiberglass substrate (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight). It is called SIBAL cloth because it was developed for the Solid Inflammability Boundary at Low-Speeds (SIBAL) spaceflight experiment and has been used in many space experiments because it burns like cotton but maintains structural integrity after the cotton is consumed. SAFFIRE-I will be conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s while SAFFIRE-III will be run at a flow velocity of 30 cm/s . In addition to the 2 samples, data was also collected for pre-flow and post-flow. These image sets are denoted as F1 for pre-flow and F2 for post-flow. The experiment data is organized in PSI by sample number and camera number. There were 2 cameras capturing images during the experiment and they are denoted as C1 for camera 1 and C2 for camera 2. There are various documents and associated information located on the different tabs within the SAFFIRE Investigations records in PSI. A very useful document to review first is the “SAFFIRE Objectives, Development and Status.pdf” document

text: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER) Abstract Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER) is an extension or continuation of Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), conducted in space from September 9 to October 5, 2007. On the success of SAME, SAMER included the following modifications: 1) a new test sample material Pyrell ®, an intumescent fire- retardant foam by Foamex was introduced to replace DBP sa mples, 2) test condition ranges was extended to include higher heating temperature and no-flow conditions, and 3) a new instrument, M-pass, developed in-house GRC, was used to replace one of the two Commercial Diagnostic Enclosures used in SAME. SAMER flight tests were conducted from July 16, to September 9, 2010, successfully completing 66 test points. As a part of SAMER effort, three major post–flight ground tests were performed: the SAMER apparatus flow tests to obtain accurate dilution ratio data, the TEM tests to obtain the 1-g counterpart of TEM samples and a batch of SMPS tests to examine the validity of the lognormal distribution assumption of aerosol particle size for the tested materials. Based on the results of both SAMER flight and ground-based tests, it is concluded that the moment method in conjunction the lognormal distribution assumption is a valid and effective ap proach to characterization of the aerosol encountered in space vehicles. Because of how they are used, a smoke detector is not calibrated for speci fic materials and instead has a single calibration for all conditions. Both figures show that the correlation decreases the relative variance by roughly a factor of at least 2 relative to that provided by a conventional single-output sensor. The resulting variance for the mass response is substantially lower than for the number concentration. This is consistent with the fact that the original optimizati on of the MPASS was to mass concentration not to number concentration. Thus with appropriate processing, the MPASS output can be proportional to either the number concentration or the mass concentration over a wide range of particle sizes and material compositions. This independence demonstrates that by combining 2 moments the MPASS is able to scale its response to the particle size being sampled giving a more accurate indication of the amount of smoke present than a single moment detector. The MPASS therefore has the ability to discern the difference between a strong signal from a high smoke concentration and a strong signal from a lower concentration of very large dust particles, a feature which can minimize false smoke detector alarms. Impact of flow on particle morphology As the samples are heated by the wire, chemical bonds are broken and gaseous products are released via pyrolysis. These products may include partially oxidized species resulting from the reaction with oxygen. As the gases move from the wire, the temperature and species concentration will decrease as a result of conduction/diffusion and convection. With the decrease in temperature, the super saturation ratio of the pyrolysis gas will pass a critical stage and nucleation of smoke particles will occur. These smoke nuclei grow rapidly from the condensation of the pyrolysis gases. The time scale for the nucleation and condensation is on the order of miliseconds or less. Over a longer time scale, the growing smoke particles undergoing Brownian motion collide and stick together in a process known as coagulation. This process may continue for time scales of up to thousand seconds. If the particles are liquid, the colliding particles will coalesce
