Maryland Project Scientist: Zengguang Yuan, National Center for Space Exploration Research Project Manager: Robert Hawersaat NASA GRC I. Introduction A. Hypothesis The hypothesis of the SPICE investi gation is that smoke point behavior will be observed for co-flowing flames and that it will show dependence on nozzle diameter and coflow velocity. B. Objectives of Investigation The objective of the SPICE experiment is to find the laminar smoke-point properties of nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the properties of the largest laminar jet diffusion flames that do not emit soot) for several fuels under different nozzle diameter/ co-flow velocity configurations. Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify models of the flame shapes under co-flow conditions. C. Previous Mission Experience N/A D. Background/History of Project (Optional) The SPICE experiment was an outgrow th of the Laminar Soot Processes Experiment (LSP) which flew on STS 83, 94, and 107. SPICE utilized the design heritage and modified the hardware from the Enclosed Laminar Flames Experiment (ELF) which flew in the Middeck Glovebox on STS 87. II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol Most tests were conducted by setting the coflow velo city, igniting the flame, and adjusting the fuel flow rate. Appr oximate smoke points were identified in the video by the flight crew and simultaneously by the ground support

Urbanc aDepartment of Fire Protection Engineering, University of Maryland, College Park, MD, USA bNational Center for Space Exploration Research, Cleveland, OH, USA cNASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH, USA Laminar smoke points were measured in nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in air coflow aboard the International Space Station as part of the Smoke Points in Coflow Experiment (SPICE). Smoke points were found for ethylene, propane, propylene, and mixtures of 50 and 75% propylene by volume in nitrogen. Burner diameters were 0.41, 0.76 and 1.6 mm and coflow velocities varied from 5.4 – 65 cm/s. These flames afford good control over residence time via variations in dilution, burner diameter , and coflow velocity. Increasing coflow velocity decreases luminous flame lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths. Smaller burners have longer smoke points for coflowing flames. These trends can be explained qualitatively by considering total residence time effects. The luminous flame lengths generally correlate with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, although they increase slightly as air velocity decreases. 1. This may be because smoke points arise from a comp etition between the times available for soot formation and soot oxidation. Quantitative correlations may also be possible from an examination of radiative losses, which have been observed to be 20 – 30% for normal-gravity smoke point flames and to increase with adiabatic flame temperature [5]. Soot is transported in flames by convection and thermophoresis. Fuel flow rate was adjusted manually and controlled with a mass flow meter. The flames were ignited with a hot-wire ignitor. Video was recorded with an analog color video camera and downlinked in real time. Still images were recorded with a 12 bit Nikon™ D100 single-lens reflex color digital still camera (with 3008 × 2000 pixels) with a 60 mm lens. Typical burn times were 60 s, and after each two such burns the MSG contents were flushed with ISS cabin air. After the tests the video record was analyzed to identify smoke point conditions. The luminous flame tips were not sharply defined in most images, but rather involved a transition from bright yellow to black across an axial distance of 2 – 5 mm. Flame hei ght was thus measured to the point where the centerline grayscale intensity changed most rapidly between these yellow and black regions. Results and Discussion Some smoke points, propane and ethylene in part icular, were identified by the onset of gradual (rather than sharp) dimming and reddening of the luminous flame tip in the downstream direction. Rounding of the tip al so was associated with th e smoke point. For conditions sufficiently above the smoke point, quenched soot could be seen leaving the flame. The brightest flames did not always display significant redden ing or darkening near their tips, except well above the smoke point. This occurred for the pu re propylene and propylene mixtures, and the smoke point was identified by the rapid transition to an open-tipped, soot emitting flame. The flames generally reached steady conditions within 5 s of ignition or a change in flow rate of fuel or air. Flames of propylene and propylene mixtures were generally more luminous than those of methane, ethylene, and propane, attribut ed to their higher propensity to form soot. The smoke point transition was more abrupt in th e propylene-based fuels than for propane or ethylene. Periodic flame motion was observed in some flames, especially those with high coflow, long length, and low fuel velocity, and is attributed to non-uniform coflow. This effect was small and did not prevent clear measurement of flame length. Figure 1 shows images for representative flames near their smoke points. Two

text: ii Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) Abstract The laminar smoke point is the condition (and the luminous flame length) where a flame begins to emit soot. Smoke points indicate the sooting propensity of a fuel in diffusion flames. In normal gravity, laminar smoke points have been measured for many gaseous and condensed fuels. Laminar smoke points have been found to correlate with soot volume fractions and radiative loss fractions of turbulent diffusion flames. SPICE project measured laminar smoke points in non) buoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in co)flowing air aboard the International Space Station. Fifty)two smoke points were found for ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene/nitrogen mixtures. Burner diameters were 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm and co)flow velocities varied from 5.4 – 65 cm/s. These flames afford extensive control over residence time via variations in dilution, burner diameter, and co)flow velocity. Increasing co)flow velocity decreases luminous flame lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths. Smaller burners have longer smoke points for co)flowing flames. These trends can be explained qualitatively by considering total residence time effects. The luminous flame lengths generally correlate with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, although they increase slightly as air velocity decreases. The measured smoke point lengths were found to correlate with burner diameter to the –0.91 power times coflow velocity to the 0.41 power. The measurements allow estimates of pseudo threshold

text: 1 INTRODUCTION SPICE project, from it was rewarded in 1997 to it was conducted onboard ISS in 2009, covered more than a decade time span. During these years, the project experienced a few cycles of active and inactive status. A brief project history is given below. SPICE project was awarded on December 3, 1997 by the Microgravity Science and Application Division of NASA Headquarters to Professor Gerard M. Faeth of the University of Michigan for his proposal titled as Laminar Smoke Point Properties of Nonbuoyant Round-Jet Diffusion Flames in response to NASA’s 1996 Solicitation for Glovebox Investigations issued in late 1996. The original proposal of Professor Faeth was meant to be a supplement to the Laminar Soot Processes Experiment which was a combustion project under NASA Grant No. NAG3-1245, conducted onboard STS-73 and STS-94 in 1997. In the awarding letter, the experiment was planned to be carried out onboard STS-107, for which the launch date was then scheduled in May 2000. From December 1997 to the end of 1999 was the first phase of the project. In this period, the experiment was planned to be conducted in the Middle Deck Glove Box of a Space Shuttle and the SPICE hardware was fabricated and assembled in GRC. Various project reviews necessary for the flight project, were completed. In addition, significant efforts on science side were made to explore proper camera settings for different flame conditions by conducting reduced gravity experiment in parabolic flight on board the KC-135 aircraft. From the end of 1999 to March 2002, the project was inactive. The second phase

text: of the project was from March 2002 to January 2005. In this period, SPICE was a part of MRDOC contract to ZIN Inc., for a potential UF-1 Flight. Since the target facility of SPICE was switched from Space Shuttle’s Middle Deck Glove Box to the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), ZIN’s major effort was to retro-fit hardware for use with MSG in International Space Station (ISS), which included: designed and assembled Power/Video Unit to support MSG video interfaces, designed and fabricated a new mechanical camera supports, redesigned fuel bottle assemblies and developed new cabling. Project was cancelled again at the end of 2004. ZIN developed storage plan for hardware which was presented to NASA in December, 2004. The SPICE apparatus was put in storage in January 2005 and all the documents were archived waiting for future flight opportunities. At that time, the LSP project and the re-flight LSP-2 were completed, thus the objectives of SPICE were later changed to a stand- alone investigation of smoke point of jet diffusion flames with coexistence of air flows. One important event soon after the SPICE became inactive again was the sudden death of Professor Faeth of the University of Michigan, the PI of the project. It was not until March 2006 that the SPICE was resurrected in May, 2006 as part of the Small Payloads Projects Task under MRDOC that Dr. David Urban, the Co-I of the project, succeeded Professor Faeth as the PI of the project. In addition, Professor Peter Sunderland of University of Maryland, former Ph.D. student of Prof. Faeth was recruited as a Co-I of the project.

text: An updated Science Requirement Document was edited. The test matrix was finalized. Additional tests in camera were conducted. Minor hardware modifications were made and a number of project reviews were conducted. The SPICE hardware was shipped to KSC on June 18, 2008 and later lifted up to ISS by ULF-2 in October 2008. SPICE experiments were finally conducted in ISS MSG from February through June of 2009. What Follows is the science significance and justification of the SPICE project. Soot formation in hydrocarbon-fueled flames is an important unresolved problem in combustion science. Soot is estimated to be responsible for up to 52,000 premature deaths annually in the U.S. 1 and is believed to contribute to climate change and glacial melting. 2 Radiation from soot in flames is beneficial in many applications but also contributes to unwanted heat loads in engines and the spread of fires. Carbon monoxide emitted by smoking flames is the major cause of death in fires. 3 Knowledge of Soot formation is needed for developing computational combustion.

Soot is estimated to be responsible for up to 52,000 premature deaths annually in the U.S. 1 and is believed to contribute to climate change and glacial melting. 2 Radiation from soot in flames is beneficial in many applications but also contributes to unwanted heat loads in engines and the spread of fires. Carbon monoxide emitted by smoking flames is the major cause of death in fires. 3 Knowledge of Soot formation is needed for developing computational combustion.

text: 2 The differences between soot processes in buoyant and nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames can be seen by comparing their soot production regions as plotted in Fig. 1. Soot formation in diffusion flames generally is limited to fuel-equivalence ratios, φ, in the range 1-2, which are marked on the plots. Unlike gases, which both convect and diffuse, soot mainly convects with the flow velocity so that it moves along the streamline. For buoyant flames, the dividing streamline generally is inside the soot formation region so that most of the soot initially forms near the flame sheet, where φ, =1, and then moves radially inward toward cooler regions having higher fuel concentrations. The soot formation process for nonbuoyant flames is completely different: most of the soot initially forms near the cool core of the flame, where φ is close to 2, and is drawn directly toward the flame sheet. Results from an MSL-1 combustion project, the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP), revealed that the smoke height phenomenon in microgravity can be substantially different form that seen in normal gravity. The removal of buoyancy induced acceleration can cause the smoke point phenomenon to be dominated by radiative heat losses for conditions of low overall flame velocity. Under these conditions the flame extinguishes at the flame tip allowing soot to be emitted. In spite of this effect, it is still possible to have flames that either emit soot along all stream lines or do not emit soot anywhere, for conditions where radiation losses do not dominate. Unfortunately, while the laminar smoke-point properties of buoyant jet diffusion flames at normal gravity are well known, corresponding information for nonbuoyant flames is limited and questionable. Thus the insights of soot generation and oxidation processes under microgravity conditions are critical to devise better fire safety strategy in spacecraft needed for long term space travels and other space exploration activities. The operation procedures are as such that the air velocity is set first, then start the fuel flow and ignite the flame. Fuel flow rate is adjusted until the smoke point is reached. Thus, for each combination of a fuel and a nozzle size, two smoke point fuel flow rates are obtained. One is under 100% air velocity and the other is under 50% air velocity. Then in the case of 50% air velocity, the fuel flow rate is reduced to 50% of the smoke point fuel flow rate to get a flame length with that fuel flow rate. SPICE EXPERIMENT SETUP A. A hot wire igniter, a coiled Kanthal wire, was used to ignite the flame. During ignition, it is moved to the nozzle tip through a handle next to the ruler handle and electrically powered up with about 4 amps of electric current that makes the wire bright red hot. Once the flame ignition is confirmed, the igniter is then moved away from the nozzle tip to its home position. The two handles are designed in such that only one of the two, the igniter and the ruler, can be moved to the nozzle at a certain time. This provides a safety feature of the system that prevents the ruler from being burned by the igniter. There is a small magnet mounted on the linkage to the igniter and a Hall-effect sensor mounted on the hinge of the front door. This sensor controls the igniter power circuits that when the front door is in open position or when the igniter is at its home position, the igniter power circuit is disabled. In other words, the igniter can be powered only if the front door is closed and the igniter is at the nozzle tip. The igniter is replaceable. It can be seen that a nozzle has two parts: a thicker base with female threads in it and a piece of thin tubing extended from the base. Thus the nozzle is threaded on a connector inside the flow duct, on the left hand side in Fig. 3. After installation, the nozzle is along the center line of flow duct. Its tip is about 54 mm from the screen at the left end of the flow duct. A thermopile radiometer, Oriel Model 71768, is placed in the far right corner downstream of the duct. It has a 90 degree view angle that can bracket the entire flame length. Since the radiometer signal is an integrated result of flame radiation, which is a complicated function of flame shape and temperature distribution in the flame, it can only provide a qualitative measurement of flame radiation. The flame radiation varies in a wide range depending on flame conditions so that the radiometer amplifier is equipped with a gain control switch to ensure the signal is detected with proper accuracy. SPICE FLIGHT TESTS The actual SPICE tests were conducted in SMG in twelve sessions from February 14, 2009 to June 23, 2009. In each session, the SPICE science team and engineering team were in the TeleScience Center (TSC) in GRC to support the tests conducted on MSG. Real-time flame images were available as long as air-to-ground communication channel was available. In addition, the team was able to communicate with the astronaut who conducted the experiment to answer questions or to clarify any ambiguities. Most tests were conducted by setting the coflow velocity, igniting the flame, and adjusting the fuel flow rate. Approximate smoke points were identified in the video by the flight crew and simultaneously by the ground support team in TSC. text: 15 Figure 17 shows images for representative flames near their smoke points. Two sequences are shown, and in both, the smoke point occurs between the third and fourth images. In the top row, coflow velocity decreases from left to right at a constant fuel flow rate. This increases luminous flame length and leads to soot emission in the fourth image. The luminous length decreases in the fourth image owing to flame extinction and extensive reactant leakage. In the bottom row, fuel flow rate is increased at a constant coflow velocity, increasing luminous lengths. The luminous lengths of the flames in Fig. 17 are more sensitive to changes in fuel flow rate than to changes in coflow velocity. For a jet diffusion flame, the fuel flow rate is the limiting factor of the flame length because there is almost unlimited amount of oxidant (air in this case) available. This is why the flame length is more sensitive to the change of fuel flow rate. In Fig. 18 the measured smoke point lengths are plotted with respect to coflow velocity. For a given choice of fuel and burner diameter, an increase in coflow velocity generally increases the smoke point length. This behavior is attributed to decreased residence times and radiative losses as coflow velocity increases, and is an important issue for further consideration. The slope of the correlations in Fig. 18 generally decreases with increased sooting propensity. Up to date, these conditions have been documented solely based on experimental observations. Many efforts have been made to develop a universal method of defining the onset of soot emission, i.e., smoke point, conditions, in terms of primary parameters of the flame. But none of these efforts has been quite successful yet. The primary parameters of the flame mentioned here refer to parameters used to set the flame, not those generated by the flame. This ratio increases with flow rate. Once it reaches about 2, smoke point occurs.15,18,19 The last surmise suggests that smoke point correlates with the centerline flame residence time. This is the most complex 8-11,17,18,20- 24 surmise because flame residence time affects the soot processes in twofold. An increase in residence time can lead to soot emissions by increasing the time available for soot formation. Because this generally also increases the time available for soot oxidation, it has been proposed that smoke points are associated with conditions where the time available for soot formation exceeds that for soot oxidation to certain extent.21 This is difficult to prove because to evaluate the flame residence time requires the velocity distribution alone the centerline and the flame length, both of which are resulted flame parameters, not readily available from primary parameters of the experiment. In addition, the soot formation time and oxidation time are conceptually defined. Practically, these times are not measurable and they might be overlapped, i.e., for the same soot aggregate, adding and oxidizing carbon particles may happen simultaneously. Because of these difficulties and ambiguities, the fame residence time theory cannot be proved or disproved rigorously. However, these obstacles do not prevent us from checking the residence time theory against the observed smoke point data

The results showed that although residence time is helpful in understanding the present smoke points, it does not yield quantitative correlations. CLOSING REMARKS Smoke points of 55 microgravity gas-jet diffusion flames in coflowing air were measured in earth orbit. The conditions emphasized small burners and the effects of coflow velocity. These flames allow extensive control over residence time, which is important in smoke point phenomena. The major conclusions are as follows: 1. An increase in coflow velocity increases the smoke point length. 2. A decrease in burner diameter increases the smoke point length. 3. These two effects can be explained qualitatively by considering residence times; increased fuel and/or coflow velocities yield increased smoke point lengths. 4. The sooting propensities of the present fuel mixtures in microgravity increase according to ethylene < propane < 50% propylene < 75% propylene < propylene. This is the same as in normal gravity except for the exchanged positions of ethylene and propane. 5. Consistent with past theory and experiments, luminous length at the smoke point is proportional to fuel mass flow rate. However there is a slight increase in luminous length as ua / u f decreases. 6. Although residence time is helpful in understanding the present smoke points, it does not yield quantitative correlations of smoke points.

Overview The Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which the tests were conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Peter B. Sunderland of the Department of Fire Protection Engineering at the University of Maryland. The two Co-Investigators (Co-Is) are Profs. Richard L. Axelbaum and Forman A. Williams who are respectively from the Washington University of St. Louis and the University of California, San Diego (UCSD). Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME including CFI-G and the rest of the ACME investigations. In ACME’s preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist. For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team included Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam who are also with CWRU. The ISS operations for CFI-G were conducted from March to Oct. 2021 in two sequential rounds of testing. The two rounds occurred during Increments 64-65 and 65-66 and respectively featured normal and inverse flames. The inverse flame tests were conducted with the chamber filled with a mixture of nitrogen and gaseous fuel while an oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowed from the burner. Overview: Cool diffusion flames were discovered in 2012 aboard the ISS. This spawned a rapidly growing research field, but only a small number of measurements at limited conditions are available. Consequently, cool flame kinetics mechanisms cannot be adequately tested or advanced. This could be impeding the development of cleaner and more efficient internal combustion engines. It is proposed here to observe cool diffusion flames supported by porous spherical burners fed with propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. Intellectual Merit: Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose understanding has large economic consequences. The proposed experiments will take advantage of many state-of-the-art diagnostics that are already available on the ISS. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. An advanced CFD model will simulate the flames and will aid the testing and development of cool flame kinetics models. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames. Each PMT will have a wide-angle view, a sight line that is orthogonal to the chamber axis, and will be centered (along the chamber length) relative to the chamber windows so that it is aligned with most of the other instrumentation. The PMTs’ spectral range will be 230-700 nm, i.e., visible and near ultraviolet, but one will have a 310-nm bandpass filter and another will have a 430-nm bandpass filter (where both are with a 10-nm FWHM). The pair of detectors will enable measurement of OH* and CH* emission, respectively. The third PMT will be equipped with a neutral density filter to prevent saturation. Like many other components, the PMT array can be removed from the chamber insert by the crew. Unlike the radiometers, each PMT had a readily adjustable gain. However, the PMT signals sometimes saturated when the gains were set too high. See the PMT Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-013) to learn more about the three Photomultiplier Tube (PMTs). The chamber insert is also equipped with six far-field thermocouples to measure the spread of the thermal field in the spherical flame experiments. They are of limited utility for other experiments because they are positioned upstream of the burner tip. The pair of detectors will enable measurement of OH* and CH* emission, respectively. The third PMT will be equipped with a neutral density filter to prevent saturation. Like many other components, the PMT array can be removed from the chamber insert by the crew. Unlike the radiometers, each PMT had a readily adjustable gain. However, the PMT signals sometimes saturated when the gains were set too high. See the PMT Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-013) to learn more about the three Photomultiplier Tube (PMTs). They are of limited utility for other experiments because they are positioned upstream of the burner tip. Therefore, they will generally not be installed by the crew to reduce the chance of accidental damage. Summary of Preliminary Results Abstract for Spherical Gas-Fueled Cool Diffusion Flames: An improved understanding of cool diffusion flames could lead to improved engines. CDFs are investigated here using a spherical porous burner with gaseous fuels in the microgravity environment of the International Space Station. Normal and inverse flames burning ethane, propane, and n-butane were explored with various fuel and oxygen concentrations, pressures, and flow rates. The diagnostics included an intensified video camera, radiometers, and thermocouples. Spherical CDFs burning gases were observed for the first time. However, these CDFs were not readily produced and were only obtained for normal n-butane flames at 2 bar with an ambient oxygen mole fraction of 0.39. The hot flames that spawned the CDFs were 2.6 times as large. An analytical model is presented that combines previous models for steady droplet burning and the partial-burning regime for CDFs. The results identify the importance of burner temperature on the behavior of these CDFs. They also indicate that the observed CDFs reside in rich regions near a mixture fraction of 0.53. Impacts, Benefits, and Products Combustion provides 86% of the world’s energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used for transportation. The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses. These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion. However, this progress is being impeded by the limited understanding of the chemistry of cool flames. Research into cool diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 – 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they were discovered in 2012. text: Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. As explained in the research proposal: Cool diffusion flames were discovered during droplet experiments aboard the International Space Station (ISS) in 2012, and this initiated a rapidly growing field of combustion research. Droplet experiments necessarily involve unsteady burning rates, so cool diffusion flames have never been observed as steady spherical flames. A natural progression toward understanding cool diffusion flames is to observe quasi-steady spherical flames on porous burners, and this is the topic of this proposal. The flames to be studied are rich in the physics and chemistry of combustion and thermal transport processes.

text: ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 29 Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose understanding has large economic consequences. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. The tests, performed with gaseous fuel and a porous spherical burner, cannot be performed in normal gravity or in ground-based microgravity facilities. CFI-G had the following experimental hypotheses and experimental objective when it was proposed in 2017: Hypotheses The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics. 1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners. 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames. Experimental Objective A. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy- driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Characteristic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. text: microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol The CFI-G investigation and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the tests were all conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. No CFI-G tests were conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. Thus far, that has been the case for all ACME tests, with the mundane exception of ‘manually’ halting the test after the flame has extinguished or perhaps if a temperature has reached a critical value. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

text: ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 31 III. Results A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight A total of 33 hot flames were ignited for the CFI-G experiment during Increment 64, where data is still be reviewed to assess the presence of cool flames. This was just the beginning of testing, which is expected to continue through most if not all of Increment 65. The CFI-G experiment does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests are independently conducted with various gaseous fuels, including ethane, propane, and n-butane. These are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the hot flame chemistry is reasonably well understood, where there is more to be learned about cool flame chemistry. No samples (e.g., of soot) were collected for CFI-G; all of the ISS results were electronically transmitted to the ground. That is furthermore the case for all currently planned ACME experiments. While nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center becomes increasing offset from the burner center. More specifically, the flame is shifted toward the supply tube indicating that the sintered attachment of the porous sphere to the supply tube is more ‘open’ than the pores of the spherical burner. text: ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 34 Burner temperatures will be analyzed to find their correlation to the cool flame diameters. E. Preliminary Research Findings [provided by the U. Maryland investigator team] The first three days of testing have yielded dozens of flames, some lasting several minutes. Based on the output from the photomultipliers, radiometers, and intensified camera images we do not believe any self-sustained cool flames were created. While it is possible that momentary cool flames were created, these are difficult to detect without increasing the gain on the intensified camera before the hot flames extinguish, which is planned. The video record will furnish excellent measurements of flame diameter versus time for a broad range of fuels and conditions. These will be compared with a simple analytical model and detailed CFD simulations using Sphdif. Thin-filament pyrometry has been performed and the results will soon be analyzed. F. Communication Imagery 1. Still Imagery Photos are available online at www.flickr.com/photos/space-flames. Although the Facebook page at www.facebook.com/space.flames is meant to provide updates on ACME and related combustion research, it is good source for recent photos, e.g., of flames, that may not be available on the Flickr site. Additional photographs may be requested from the Project Scientist, Dennis Stocker (dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov). 2. text: Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) experiment are conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. As explained in the research proposal: Cool diffusion flames were discovered during droplet experiments aboard the International Space Station (ISS) in 2012, and this initiated a rapidly growing field of combustion research. Droplet experiments necessarily involve unsteady burning rates, so cool diffusion flames have never been observed as steady spherical flames. A natural progression toward understanding cool diffusion flames is to observe quasi-steady spherical flames on porous burners, and this is the topic of this proposal. The flames to be studied are rich in the physics and chemistry of combustion and thermal transport processes.

text: ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 36 Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose understanding has large economic consequences. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. The tests, performed with gaseous fuel and a porous spherical burner, cannot be performed in normal gravity or in ground-based microgravity facilities. CFI-G had the following experimental hypotheses and experimental objective when it was proposed in 2017: Hypotheses The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics. 1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners. 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames. Experimental Objective A. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate. where

Characteristic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Methods/Research Operations B. Discussion of Method/Protocol The CFI-G investigation and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the tests were all conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. No CFI-G tests were conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. Thus far, that has been the case for all ACME tests, with the mundane exception of ‘manually’ halting the test after the flame has extinguished or perhaps if a temperature has reached a critical value. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

Mission anomalies On Aug. 30 (GMT 242), the primary Image Processing and Storage Unit, used to record the imaging from both the ACME DataCam and CFI intensified camera (IPSU-G, also known as IPSU5), caused issues and eventually stopped working. Only the first two tests on that day were successful, where two tests aborted due to an IPSU error, and three tests failed to ignite. In closing checkout, it was determined that the hot-wire igniter tip had also failed. With the IPSU-G failure, the test day was nearly a total loss. Except for a small number of sample images downloaded during the midst of testing, the primary image data from even the successful tests was lost. Furthermore, there was no more propane available for use in inverse-flame testing, so the test day could not be repeated. However, astronaut Mark Vande Hei replaced the failed igniter tip on Sept. 8 and the failed hard drive in the IPSU-G on Sept. 10, and CFI-G testing successfully resumed on Sept. 13, just 2 weeks after the double failure. Looking back to Increment 64, the Image Processing and Storage Unit (IPSU1) used with the High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera and the opposed CIR illumination package ceased functioning on March 29 (GMT 088). Tests 21088M1-M3 aborted due to an error with IPSU1 communication, where test M4 was successful when the test was run without use of the HiBMs camera. The troublesome IPSU1 was replaced by astronaut Megan McArthur on May 18 (GMT 138), but it was not available

Recovery plans were developed and enacted on 18 Jan. 2021 to remove the broken fragments from the harp-like array. Completeness/Quality of Data The experiment’s proposal to CASIS and NSF stated: “It is assumed here that approximately 50 ISS flames can be conducted. These will include approximately 12 chamber fills following evacuation.” Far more testing was carried out for this experiment, where that included the ignition of 280 hot flames in 23 days of ISS testing, some of which included multiple chamber fills. Although some of the flames were short lived, the testing far exceeded the quantity that had been proposed. The cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually become ‘hot’ (i.e., dead) over time. While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing, they are a degradation of the image quality. It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there is not obvious indication of this; and it has thus far not been evaluated with available measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS). Recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking. This is done because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be managed per test day. Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice some image data to allow additional tests to be conducted. This is intentionally done to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing within the project constraints. J. text: of the fuel mass flow rate (for normal flames), the oxidizer mass flow rate (for inverse flames), O2 concentration, fuel dilution, and pressure were obtained for all the normal and inverse flame test days. The raw test measurements made from devices - such as thermocouples, photomultiplier tubes (PMTs), gas flow meters, and radiometers - were saved in a csv file format per each test. The data rate of the non-imaging measurements was 125 per sec. The raw data was processed to transform it into scientific measurements. The transformed data were visualized as plots for further analysis. In addition, test images recorded in tiff and hobj formats respectively for the CFI intensified camera and ACME DataCam have been analyzed to investigate the presence of cool flames and to find flame diameters. Of these the intensified camera is of most value, and all of its images to date have been converted to video files and reviewed. Since the intensified camera images were taken under the maximum possible gain applied, the images were averaged and filtered to decrease the overall noise level, and the intensity of the images was increased by a factor of 50 to facilitate the search of intensity peaks.

text: ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 44 Particular attention has been given to the PMT-2 measurements due to its sensitivity to wavelengths of 230 – 700 nm for CH2O* to investigate the presence of cool flames. PMT- 2 measurements have been analyzed to determine flame durations as well. Because cool diffusion flames were identified through the readings of radiometers after the radiative extinction of hot flames, the radiometer data was carefully analyzed. Burner temperatures were analyzed to find their correlation to the ignition and diameter of cool flames. K. Preliminary Research Findings [provided by the U. of Maryland investigator team and lightly edited by Stocker] A total of 280 hot diffusion flames were observed. Among them, 189 flames experienced radiative extinction, and the rest were extinguished when their flow was terminated, either because the preset flow time was out or the burner overheated. Of those that extinguished radiatively, 15 subsequently reignited as cool diffusion flames. These cool flames were observed only with the following conditions: a) concentrations of 30 vol% n- butane and 40 vol% O2, b) normal flames, c) a pressure of 2.03 bar, and d) mass flow rates between 0.75 – 1.5 mg/s. Cool diffusion flames were initially identified by the readings of radiometers after the radiative extinction of hot flames. Unlike the heat flux shown in Fig. 1(a), Fig. 1(b) shows that the radiant heat flux did not drop to zero after the radiative extinction of a hot flame. Instead, it decreased to a certain level and stayed at that level until the fuel stopped

text: ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 51 Appendix F. ISS Operations per the Payload Weekly Science Summary 2021 (for all of CFI-G) First round (normal flames) Increment 64 Week 21: March 5-11 On GMT 062, the final test points were performed for ACME CLD Flame (Coflow Laminar Diffusion). The Principal Investigator, Marshall Long from Yale University, considers the experiment to have been very successful. On this day, 11 flames were ignited, which contributed to the over 300 that were ignited for all of CLD Flame. Early results show that the dilution limits are extended in microgravity compared to normal gravity. Steady microgravity flames are also more stable and have lower lift-off heights due to the lack of buoyancy. We have gathered a superior set of experimental data to be used for improving our ability to computationally model highly diluted flames. This capability could be implemented in design tools resulting in more efficient and less polluting combustion here on Earth. On GMT 068 & 069, Kate Rubins configured the ACME Chamber Insert to support the next ACME experiment, CFI-G Part 1 (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases). CFI-G will study flames with unusually low temperatures known as cool flames. These flames were discovered in 2012 with the first subrack payload to use CIR, but this investigation only used liquid fuels. ACME’s hardware will allow CFI-G to study gaseous fuels to gain valuable insight into the combustion processes in engines. The time-lapse CLD Flame image associated with this submission is not included in this report. Week 22: March 12-18

These tasks prepared the CIR for supporting the next ACME experiment, CFI-G Part 1 (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases). CFI-G will study flames with unusually low temperatures known as cool flames. Week 24: March 26 – April 1 On GMT 088, the first test points were performed for ACME CFI-G Part 1 (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases) with 14 ethane flames, sometimes diluted with nitrogen, ignited in various oxygen/nitrogen atmospheres. CFI-G studies flames with unusually low temperatures known as cool flames, which were discovered in 2012 with droplet combustion research being conducted in CIR at the time. That experiment burned liquid fuel droplets, which shrink as they burn. Instead, CFI-G will burn gaseous fuel ejected from a porous spherical burner to investigate cool flames under quasi-steady conditions. Cool flame chemical kinetics are important to ignition and the results could lead to cleaner burning and more efficient internal combustion engines.

Preliminary False-Colored Image of Hot Ethane Flame for CFI-G This false-colored image shows a spherical flame, which is only possible in microgravity without the buoyant flows created by Earth’s gravity. Spherical flames greatly simplify experimental analysis by reducing the flame structure to a single dimension, which allows computational models to focus on chemical kinetics and transport phenomena. The hot flame in Figure 1 has a hole at the bottom because of heat loss to the fuel tube, which supplies the ethane to the porous sphere. The three bright lines passing through the flame are 14-micron ceramic fibers, which were translated into the flame to determine temperature measurements from the color of the glowing fibers. Residual soot clusters, like the fibers, are glowing because of their high temperature. These soot clusters were “pushed” to the bottom half of the flame by the insertion of the fibers. Week 26: April 9-15 On GMT 102, nine nitrogen-diluted butane flames were ignited for ACME CFI-G (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases). Non-premixed (i.e., fuel and oxidizer are not mixed prior to reacting) cool flames were discovered in 2012 with CIR droplet combustion research using liquid fuels. CFI-G’s goal is to study non- premixed cool flames using gaseous fuels, which have not been observed before and so far have not been observed in CFI-G testing. It is still possible that they may be detected in a more thorough review of the data. Whether cool flames are present or not, we are still acquiring useful results,

text: ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 55 Figure 1. CFI-G Hot Flame of Nitrogen-Diluted Propane Figure 1 shows images of a CFI-G hot flame from two different cameras. The left image is from a color camera. The right image, which has been false-colored, is from an intensified camera filtered for formaldehyde (CH2O) emissions, which are associated with cool flame chemistry. When cool flames were first discovered in 1809, Sir Humphrey Davy observed a “pale phosphorescent light.” Residual soot created during ignition escapes from opposite sides of the flame. Week 11: June 18-24 On GMT 174, we ignited 16 nitrogen-diluted butane flames in the final tests for the first round of ACME CFI-G (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases). Cool flames remained elusive, where there has been no clear evidence of these low-temperature phenomena during this round of testing. In the coming weeks and months, we will review the data more closely to assess their potential presence. Regardless, we gathered a wealth of valuable data that will improve our fundamental understanding of soot process and flame dynamics. Since CFI-G tested with different fuels, these data expand upon the results gained from the other ACME experiments. Next week, the ACME Chamber Insert will be configured to support the second and final round of CFI-G testing. This testing will explore the potential existence of cool flames in an inverse configuration. The flow direction will be reversed, where a mixture of nitrogen and oxygen will flow from the burner into the Combustion Chamber, which will be filled with a mixture of nitrogen and gaseous fuel. As a result, the flames will be inside out, where, as an example, the soot will be formed outside of the flame.

Composite Image of CFI-G Inverse Flames at Increasing Flow Rates This composite image compares inverse flames with multiples of oxygen/nitrogen flow rates from the porous spherical burner faintly seen within the flames. The oxygen flows outward until it reaches sufficient fuel to be consumed. As such, the tests with the greater oxidizer flow rates result in larger flames. Radiative heat loss scales with flame size, and the larger flames are dimmer than the smaller flames. The oxygen/nitrogen ratio, propane concentration, and Combustion Chamber pressure were consistent in this trio of tests. These flames are locally quenched by heat loss to the burner’s supply tube leaving an opening in the flame. The opening, which allows reactant mixing, often oscillates in size while growing until the flame fully extinguishes. In some tests the extinction occurs abruptly, but in others the oscillations can last for tens of seconds. Meanwhile, some flames are quasi-steady despite the opening. The other test parameters included changing the flow rate and ratio of the oxygen/nitrogen mixture issuing from the burner. This marks the completion of CFI-G Part 2! Figure 1. Example CFI-G Inverse Butane Flame This example image can be readily identified as an inverse flame because the soot is outside, rather than inside, of the flame. The soot is formed when the fuel combines with itself at high temperatures in the absence of oxygen. In this regard, the inverse flame is like a bubble separating the outer fuel from the inner oxygen, where the two reactants are consumed producing light, heat, and chemical products (e.g., carbon dioxide and water vapor). Flames of hydrocarbon fuels are naturally blue, while the high- temperature soot glows red, orange, yellow, or even white depending on its temperature. At ignition, this flame was all bright and sooty, but the system is not fully symmetric. There is some asymmetry to the burner flow, and there is heat loss to the tube supplying the gas to the porous spherical burner. As a result, the soot faded from the lower hemisphere, which in this image appears to be soot free. Meanwhile, the upper hemisphere remained enveloped in a layer of glowing soot. Tests like this have yielded valuable data for improving our understanding of how to control soot generation. text: ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 67 Increment 66 Week 1: Oct. 15-21 On GMT 291, we performed the last 12 tests for ACME CFI-G (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases) during an extra day of testing with normal flames. The purpose of this extra day was to recreate the test conditions in which we achieved cool flames in earlier testing, and we successfully achieved cool flames! In two tests, the butane hot flames extinguished due to radiative heat loss, but then seconds later they reignited. This extinction and reignition occurred several times during each of these tests. The butane reignited because a cool flame occurred between the hot flames. Cool flame chemistry is important for ignition in internal combustion engines and an improved understanding would aid the development of vehicles that experience less wear on engine parts, get better gas mileage, and create less pollution. text: ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 86 Appendix M. Summary of the ISS data collection The CFI-G data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where this is true for the other ACME experiments. To be clear, there was no collection of soot or other physical samples that were subsequently transported to the ground. The CFI-G image data includes images from the following cameras: 1. ACME DataCam, used with a clear fused-silica ‘filter’ and various zoom and focus settings (but those settings were consistent within each individual test) 2. CFI intensified camera, used always (or at least nearly so) with a formaldehyde filter for CFI-G 3. High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a red filter corresponding to the opposing CIR illumination package, which was sometimes left off The raw DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic Object (hobj) format, while the images from the CFI, and HiBMs cameras are provided in a Tagged Image File (tif) format. In contrast, the analog video was recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). The raw data is currently archived at NASA and work is underway to make it available publicly through NASA’s Physical Science Informatics System (PSI).

While general to ACME, the article addresses CFI-G with a statement about the flames: “In microgravity they can swell into ethereal … orbs that can burn at a surprisingly cool 900 degrees Fahrenheit (a gas stove burner’s high setting is about 3100oF).” Despite its brevity, Sunderland and Stocker were both interviewed for the article. Stocker is involved in a broad range of NASA educational outreach to students and teachers, Scouts of both genders, and the general public. His primary outreach focus is the fundamentals of microgravity and human spaceflight, for example through microgravity design challenges which he helps create and administer. But he periodically addresses other topics, e.g., where he sometimes speaks on ‘NASA and the Science of Superman’ – for example at the Superman Celebration in Metropolis, IL. In this regard, his NASA outreach is carried out locally, regionally, nationally, and online. For example, he regularly presents on microgravity at Space Center Houston’s Space Exploration Educators Conference (SEEC). He has exhibited the last five National Scout Jamborees, five national Boy Scout conferences, the last three national Girl Scout conventions, and the 2019 World Scout Jamboree (which was held in the U.S.). Stocker has been a key lead for the agency in NASA’s participation in these Scouting events, where as an example the latter outreach is visually described at www.nasa.gov/feature/stem/world-scout-jamboree.html.

text: purpose of s-Flame is to advance the ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction and instabilities, of both soot-free and sooty flames. The results may contribute to the development of lean-burn engines for improved efficiency and reduced pollutant emissions here on Earth. The spherical flames are ignited at non-steady conditions and allowed to transition naturally towards steady-state or extinction. Tests are conducted with various inert diluents in both the fuel and chamber (oxidizer) atmosphere. The fuel gases include hydrogen and methane mixtures for soot-free flames, and ethylene for sooty flames. One experimental objective is to identify the extinction limits for both radiative and chemical kinetic extinction, i.e., where the flame extinguishes from radiative heat loss or is “blown out,” respectively. Another objective is to determine the existence, onset, and nature of pulsating instabilities that have been theoretically predicted to occur in flames with certain fuel/inert mixtures at near-limit conditions.

text: ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63 3 II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol The s-Flame investigation and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the tests were all conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. As expected, no s-Flame tests were conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. Thus far, that has been the case for all ACME tests, with the mundane exception of ‘manually’ halting the test after the flame has extinguished or perhaps if a temperature has reached a critical value. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing. III. Results A. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data Ignition of the flames presented a significant challenge to the experiment during this increment. All of the flame tests were conducted where the fuel and chamber atmosphere were both diluted with helium rather than the nitrogen used in Increments 60 and 61. The two gases’ properties are dramatically different making comparison testing very desirable for manifestation of different phenomena. Helium’s thermal conductivity is notably several times greater than that of nitrogen, so considerably more energy and power was required to ignite the flames. The power level was slowly increased from test to test until ignition was finally achieved on the ninth test, where only seven flames were ignited of the 15 tests conducted on May 11 (20132), the first day for flames in Increment 63. The cautious approach was taken because of concerns that the igniter tip might fail (i.e., burn out) if too much power was applied. At high flow rates, the burner does not produce spherically symmetric flames. While nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center becomes increasing offset from the burner center. More specifically, the flame is shifted toward the supply tube indicating that the sintered attachment of the porous sphere to the supply tube is more ‘open’ than the pores of the spherical burner. In other words, the flow from the burner is not spherically symmetric. At sufficiently high flow rates, the flame becomes obviously non-spherical, where it can appear to be ellipsoidal or even parabolic in shape. At 5 and 5.5 cc/s, nice blue chemiluminescent flames were ignited, but eventually were cut off because of the burner temperature limit being reached. At 6 cc/s, a nice blue flame was ignited which expanded slowly to extinction. At 7, 10, and 15 cc/s, sooty ignition occurred, but as the flames expanded, the soot went away, eventually resulting in radiative extinction. By ramping the flow rates up, starting at 5 cc/s, soot at ignition was minimized, and the flames could expand to extinction. Ramp down of the flow rate resulted in almost immediate extinction. For tests at 21% O2/He atmosphere, cases at 5, 10, and 15 cc/s resulted in flames that expanded quickly to extinction. Less soot was present at ignition compared with that for the 30% O2/He atmosphere cases. Consistent ignition was not always achieved for the same conditions, which is puzzling. At 6, 7, 10, and 15 cc/s, the flames were sooty at ignition, but the soot dissipated; and they expanded to extinction. Ramping up the flow rates, starting at 5 cc/s, minimized soot at ignition and resulted in flames that slowly expanded to extinction. text: ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 3 1. Overview The Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which tests are conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). text: July 2020. 2. Science Overview A. Background This background is the Executive Summary from the experiment’s Science Requirements Document (SRD) of Jan. 2010. Recognizing that most combustion engines and devices operate on the basis of diffusion flames, the proposed program aims to characterize and gain predictive capability of the structure and dynamics of diffusion flames in simple, well-defined flow fields such that the phenomena of interest can be studied without being unduly complicated and compromised by complex and sometimes non-quantifiable flow field effects. The basic flame configuration adopted for the investigation is the spherically symmetric diffusion flame generated by discharging a fuel gas from a porous spherical burner into a quiescent, oxidizing ambience in microgravity. The one- dimensional nature of the system facilitates data acquisition, data reduction, and computational simulation. The primary goals of the program are two-fold and strongly interdependent. The first objective is to interrogate the fidelity of the chemical kinetic mechanisms and transport submodels used in the simulation of aerothermochemical phenomena, and consequently identify possible modifications. The second objective is to characterize and gain predictive capability on spherical diffusion flames.

text: ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 4 The space flight program consists of two main parts: (1) Mapping and characterization of the movement of spherical diffusion flames subsequent to ignition from a non-steady-state condition and their extinction boundaries due to direct finite-rate chemistry and indirect radiative heat loss. The emphases are on the relative importance of radiative emission and re-absorption, the examination of the adequacy of the detailed chemical kinetics mechanism and transport sub- models used, and the development of flame front instabilities that could modify the extinction boundaries. Results of the study are of relevance to the development of lean-burn engines for improved efficiency and reduced pollutant emissions. (2) Studies of the response of characteristically sooty flames to a non-steady-state initial condition with respect to the aspects given in (1). The studies will include characterizing soot onset as a function of residence time for expanding flames, as well as soot radiation and transport contributions in spreading, extinction, and instability. The project involves microgravity experimentation, computational simulation, and, where appropriate, theoretical analysis. Interpretation of all phenomena will emphasize the simultaneous and coupled influence of chemistry and transport. B. text: of Terrestrial (1g laboratory) Testing We seek to make observations of truly one-dimensional flames whose structure can be studied without complications due to uncertainties in the flow pattern caused by buoyancy. Such fundamental study of flame structure and dynamics is best served via the elimination of buoyancy through the reduction of gravity. The minimum sizes of these flames imply that buoyancy would be significant if the experiments were conducted in normal gravity. Previous experimentation on earth has amply demonstrated this influence. Although studies of spherical diffusion flames were conducted in normal gravity using the low-pressure, inverse-flame arrangement (see §1), the conditions are limited for small flames, low pressures, low molecular weight fuels. Indeed, only the hydrogen flame can be considered to be nearly buoyancy free. With such constraints, normal-pressure, micro-gravity, hydrocarbon-based experiments are requisite. One-dimensional spherical flames allow for the unambiguous study of such fundamental flame phenomena as the dynamics and extinction of diffusion flames (including the mechanisms of flame front unsteadiness), soot suppression/formation, and flame front instabilities, without gravity-induced baroclinicity and buoyancy, on the flame responses.

Although experimental data of good quality were obtained on the transient response of spherical diffusion flames in the 2.2-s drop tower facility, the duration was insufficient to observe radiative extinction. The numerical simulations indicate that, for the characteristic flames under study, more than 2.5s of microgravity time is needed. Subsequent parabolic aircraft experimentation afforded the additional low-gravity duration (up to 10s by free-floating the apparatus), as well as an experimental package incorporating rainbow schlieren (which cannot be contained within a package for the 2.2-s drop tower), although radiative extinction was still not observed. The unavoidable g-jitter associated with the facility, however, renders the observation less definitive. Note that even though the package was free-floated, umbilical restrictions could not be avoided. The comprehensiveness of these mechanisms has been extensively tested for premixed but not diffusion flames, especially in simple, well-defined flow fields not complicated by buoyant flows. A burner-generated spherical diffusion flame provides a simple, one-dimensional flame geometry that permits a rigorous comparison between detailed theory and experimental verification. Existing theory and limited low-gravity experimental results suggest that quasi-steady spherical diffusion flames can exist with some combinations of fuel mixture supply rates and quiescent ambient oxidizers. With respect to the steady flame conditions, altering fuel supply rates to limit flame residence time induces a convective-kinetic extinction limit. Alternatively, very large residence times allow radiative heat losses and diffusive transport mechanisms to quench the flame. Near these dual flammability boundaries of quasi-steady flames, flame-front instabilities may appear before the flame is quenched. As depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4 to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1 and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and two flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm). Most burners will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux transducers. The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring of the pressure differential across the outlet surface. The igniter will have a crew-exchangeable tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper-motor drive will allow for precise positioning. text: chamber and a standard analog camera mounted on the chamber insert (with a turning mirror). Both cameras are part of the ACME hardware that is now in development. The analog camera signal will be downlinked in near real time to support the experiment operations. Light- emitting diodes within the chamber can be used to illuminate the igniter and burner to both support the operations and provide reference images. The 12-bit digital camera records at up to 30 full frames (1360x1024) per second, and is equipped with a motorized lens with independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus. The digital camera will be equipped with a filter assembly with four options, where selection of a clear “filter” allows for color imaging. Color imaging can also be carried out with a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, which balances the color planes to avoid saturation in the red while maintaining sensitivity in the blue and green. The natural flame color can be approximately reconstructed, but the primary purpose of the filter is pyrometry and measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniques of [23-24]. Alternately, CH* imaging can be conducted with this camera because the filter assembly includes a 430-nm bandpass filter with a 10-nm full width at half-maximum transmission (FWHM). A 450-nm bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively subtract interfering broadband soot emission. However, the filter assembly rotates slowly so such subtraction effectively requires a separate test with each filter and of course reproducible flame conditions.

To be clear, the acceleration measurements are not archived with the ACME experiment data in the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) website, www.nasa.gov/PSI. All ACME experiments will be constant volume (i.e., rather than constant pressure) studies, where the chamber’s free volume will be about 90 liters. Burner flows will generally be constrained to limit the pressure rise, and tests will typically be 0.5-2 minutes in duration. The chamber’s free volume is approximately 83 liters depending on the installed hardware. The ACME experiments will be configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. Instead, the experiments will be commanded from the ground, specifically from the Telescience Support Center (TSC) at the NASA Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, Ohio. They can be conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it will also be possible to effectively operate the experiments in a “manual” mode, where changes can be made in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. For example, a flow rate could be adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit. Step and ramp changes can be made in the flow rate(s) or electric field potential. The TFP fiber array can be translated uniformly through a soot-free flame to get a continuum measurement of the temperature field. In summary, ACME’s experiment control will allow for broad flexibility. The TSC is now also referred to as the Glenn

Hardware Shortcomings Key s-Flame shortcomings include image acquisition, limited imaging sensitivity (especially to the hydrogen flames), and the flow asymmetry from the burner (especially at high flow rates). Other shortcomings are discussed in this section and Appendices B to D, but the reader may want to refer to the ACME Engineering Implementation document for additional information. At high flow rates, the porous spherical burner used for s-Flame did not produce spherically symmetric flames. While they were nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center became increasing offset from the burner center when testing with higher flow rates. More specifically, the flame shifted toward the supply tube indicating that the sintered attachment of the porous sphere to the supply tube is more ‘open’ than the pores of the sintered sphere. In other words, the flow from the burner is not spherically symmetric. At sufficiently high flow rates, the flame becomes obviously non-spherical, where it can appear to be ellipsoidal or even parabolic in shape. In the latter case, the flame locally quenches near the supply tube. When s-Flame’s first fuel bottle was installed on 30 July 2019 (19211), it was at the expected pressure, but the fuel pressure was observed to drop with time, indicating a leak. Troubleshooting, including testing with other fuel bottles, was carried out and it was concluded that the leak was related to the bottle’s quick connection

text: ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021 25 C. Summary of Preliminary Results The s-Flame experiment aims to characterize and gain predictive capability of the structure and dynamics of diffusion flames in simple, well-defined flow fields such that the phenomena of interest can be studied without being complicated by various flow field effects. The basic flame configuration adopted for the investigation is the spherically symmetric diffusion flame generated by discharging a fuel gas from a porous spherical burner into a quiescent, oxidizing atmosphere in microgravity. The theoretically one-dimensional nature of the system facilitates data acquisition, data reduction, and computational simulation. The s-Flame experiment uses the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the ACME hardware in the Destiny module of the ISS. Specifically, the s-Flame tests are intended to: (i) Advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of both soot-free and sooty flames; (ii) Obtain experimental data in simple, well-defined flow fields and understand various key elemental diffusion flame processes; (iii) Identify the extinction limits for both radiative and convective extinction (i.e., at high and low system Damköhler numbers, respectively); (iv) Determine the existence, onset, and nature of pulsating instabilities that have been theoretically predicted to occur in such flames with fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number; (v) Validate and/or improve accuracy of computational simulation including detailed chemistry and transport. The project

As seen in Table 1, the first round of tests examined nitrogen-diluted fuel burning in a nitrogen- diluted oxidizing atmosphere. Test day 19254 examines nitrogen-diluted C2H4 issuing into 21% O2 / 79% N2 atmosphere. C2H4 allows for the examination of a fuel with nominal unity Le number, setting a baseline standard for flame stretch and thermal diffusive stability effects. Additionally, its characteristic sooting nature (in normal gravity) directly addresses our basic science objectives focusing on spreading of flame sheets, dual extinction states, and flame-front instabilities. For a case of fuel-mixture of 20% C2H4 / 80% N2 at a flow rate of 3 cc/s, a seemingly quasi-steady flame is attained for extended duration. For the same mixture, higher flow rates of 5-10 cc/s result in radiative extinctions, corresponding to high system Damköhler number. Other mixtures of 25% C2H4 / 75% N2 and 30% C2H4 / 70% N2, also show radiative extinctions at higher flow rates. Since characteristic residence times will affect sooting tendencies, various flow rates are investigated for different mixtures. Soot is only observed during ignition, which goes away as the flames establish themselves, as seen for cases where low flow rates (e.g., 3 cc/s) with low ethylene contents (e.g., 25-30% C2H4) are ramped to high flow rates (e.g., 5-10 cc/s) with higher ethylene contents (e.g., 40-50% C2H4). Soot will also enhance flame radiation, but our non-sooty flames already extinguish as they spread outwardly. Observations

G. Impacts, Benefits, and Products The impact of this work consists of both practical and fundamental aspects. Practically, with diffusion flame burning as the basis in many combustion engines and devices, understanding the underlying dynamics and chemistry of diffusion flames is important in improving performance in terms of power, efficiency, pollutant emissions, and reliability. Fundamentally, the unique buoyancy-free environment offered by microgravity affords simple aerodynamic flow fields to acquire diffusion flame data of high fidelity, with the prospect of understanding unit thermochemical processes as well as quantifying the associated physico-chemical parameters. In analyzing and validating the data sets, the experimental data and corresponding computational simulations should yield quantitative and qualitative understanding of various elemental flame phenomena. In studying the transient motion of diffusion flames ignited from a non-steady-state initial condition, the significance of fuel accumulation will be evaluated, which was originally found to be important in droplet burning. Here, with no droplet surface regression nor coupling of fuel flow to heat transfer from the flame to influence flame-front motion, the effect can be better isolated

Quantitative predictability of the flame motion permits assessment of the parameters and mechanisms involved in radiation loss and re- absorption as well as other transport parameters. The microgravity environment greatly facilitates the examination of pulsating instabilities, which can be hidden or coupled to other processes in normal gravity. Moreover, involvement of multi-dimensional effects, rather than the nominally 1-D geometry here, would further complicate the manifestation of the phenomenon. Near-limit phenomena, including extinction, is best evaluated and validated using our one- dimensional spherical diffusion flame (as realized in the microgravity environment), which is probably the most desirable flame configuration for study of this nature. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies.
