D.4 Background The basis for the burning rate estimates presented here are based on both a computational study looking at the burning rate distribution for boundary layer flow combustion of a PMMA plate in forced flow, shown in Figure D.1, (Ref. 1), and BASS test results from a 1-cm PMMA sphere burning in a stagnation flow (which captures the burning of the exposed base of the sample). A thick PMMA slab will take time to ignite and grow to a steady-state size, and the sample burning rate distribution is an important quantity to determine how much heat is being generated by the flame. D.5 Analysis As can be seen in Figure D.2, the base of the flame (at x = 0) has the highest burning rate and there is an exponential decay in the regression rate away from that peak burning rate. Using peak regression rate (rmax) for the four flow profiles given, we can extrapolate down to the 30-cm/s flow of interest. The exposed base of the flame (the upstream most point) will be the strongest part of the flame, and the burning rate is expected to be a maximum there. Based on data in the Section D.7 from a 1-cm-sphere BASS test, we estimate the regression rate to be 3.05 mm/min, which is in keeping with the estimates from Figure D.2, as shown in Figure D.3. The downstream regression rates will decay exponentially from there, as shown in Figure D.2.

text: NASA/TM-20210011385 123 Figure D.2.—Peak regression rates from Figure D.2 curve fit with expected square root trend as flow is reduced (Ref. 2). Fit is used to calculate extrapolated points. At 30 cm/s, peak regression rate is estimated to be 3.13 mm/min. Figure D.3.—Power law growth pattern used to predict flame size as function of time. The sample is 8.5 cm long, so at 3.05 mm/min, it will take ~28 min for the flame base to regress the entire length of the sample. Note that this is way beyond the still camera card limit of 7 min. The flame will take some time to grow the steady-state size. To estimate the growth rate, we use an expected power law growth rate (Ref. 3) and estimate the flame will grow to a steady-state size in approximately 2.5 min, as shown in Figure D.3. This growth rate is quite reasonable, since a previous BASS test showed that a PMMA slab sample took over 3 min to grow to steady size, as shown in the Section D.7. Using the experimental growth history and peak regression rates, we can estimate the regression rate profiles as a function of time. These regression profiles (which occur on both sides of the sample) can then be used to determine how much fuel is being consumed each minute. We do this by adding up the regression at each x location (basically, the area under the curves) and also multiplying that value by the width of the sample (2 cm). Note that these profiles are derived from steady slab burning where a significant fraction of the heat release is returned to the fuel for preheating or reradiated to the environment.

text: NASA/TM-20210011385 126 The maximum burn time is assumed to be the 2.5-min growth phase plus the 28-min sample regression phase, for a total of 30.5 min, as plotted in Figure D.5. The maximum temperatures reported in the following information are for this maximum burn time. The heat release in the early phase is dominated by the ignition energy. Once the combustion heat release approaches steady state, the igniter is turned off and the flame is sustained. The maximum temperature will occur in the exhaust hardware. This metal (primarily copper) hardware is built to take the hot combustion gases and cool via conduction to the other hardware. The maximum temperature if all of the combustion energy is only deposited in this heat sink under these worst-case assumptions, is 434 °C, which is below the melting point of the lowest melting material (aluminum at 660 °C) so this absolute worst-case maximum temperature will not cause damage to the hardware. This maximum temperature will not be realized in actuality because the heat will quickly dissipate to the main housing, which reaches a maximum temperature of 110 °C if all of the heat is distributed only there. The experiment assembly dissipates the heat further, and the maximum temperature of the entire experiment assembly is 62 °C. During the 10-min cooldown for these thick samples, both the flow through the BASS duct and the MSG air circulation fans help dissipate the heat. text: NASA/TM-20210011385 127 D.7 Appendix—Polymethylmethacrylate Growth to Steady Size In Figure D.6, a one-sided PMMA slab was burned at a slow flow. The 1-cm-wide sample took 7.5 min for the total test time, with the ignition taking over 1 min. Flame reached steady size in about 3 min and was only 15 mm long. The spread rate was 0.037 mm/s (0.0037 cm/s or 2.2 mm/min). The BASS 1-cm sphere had an initial mass of 617.5 mg. Sample 19 (1-cm PMMA sphere) was completely consumed in four tests (various high- and low-flow speeds) with the burn durations in Table D.2. The total burn time was 5 min and 25 s (325 s). The average burning rate was 617.5/325 = 1.9 mg/s. Assume this occurs over the surface of the sphere where A = 4πr2 = 3.14 × 0.52 × 4 = 3.14 cm2. So, 1.9 mg/s ÷ 1.19 mg/mm3 ÷ 314 mm2 = 0.005 mm/s × 60 s/min = 0.3 mm/min. Note this is 0.0005 cm/s, which is equivalent to a stretch rate of 10 s–1, a reasonable 0g level for burning rates for PMMA from (Ref. 4) as seen in Figure D.7. Figure D.6.—Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) one-sided polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) slab burn at slower flow, 1-cm-wide sample.

Overview The CFI experiments are conceived as follow-up experiments to the FLEX and FLEX-2 droplet combustion experiments onboard the ISS to further explore the newly discovered quasi-steady “cool flames.” Cool flames are controlled by low temperature chemistry, and occur in the NTC region of n-alkane fuels. FLEX series of experiments showed for the first time that quasi-steady stable flames can be established surrounding a droplet in microgravity under certain conditions, without a visible flame at temperatures in the range of 700 to 900 K, unlike the hot flames where the flame temperature is higher than 1200 K. Since the cool-flame chemistry depends on the chemical structure of the fuel as well as pressure and temperature, three different fuel combinations were investigated, namely, pure n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso- dodecane mixtures and farnesane ( a renewable jet fuel) at ambient pressures up to 5 atmospheres. Cool flame extinction occurs when its static stability is lost close to the lower turnover point in the NTC

Subsequently, a droplet of desired size is dispensed between the hypodermic needles and freely deployed, and ignited. The igniter is withdrawn from the FOV once ignition is detected. When required a 40 micron silicon-carbide fiber is used to tether the droplet at one place and stop it from drifting off from the field of view. The combustion process is recorded using a backlit, black-and-white camera ( 5 cm X 5 cm FOV) to obtain droplet size as a function of time, a UV-sensitive camera is used to image the OH* emission from the flame which provides the flame size data. A color camera which is had a live downlink to the TSC is used to perform and monitor the overall process. Narrow-band and wide-band radiometers are used to measure the radiation emission from the flame. Details of the experimental hardware and the data reduction procedures can be found in Dietrich et al. (2014) b. On-Orbit Testing Over two hundred tests were carried out during the CFI experimental campaign. The initial droplet size was kept around 4 mm so that radiative extinction and the subsequent cool flame combustion can be observed. As the droplet size decreases, the residence time in the reaction zone of the gas-phase diffusion flame is reduced to a value corresponding to which the cool flame becomes statically unstable, and this leads to cool flame extinction. Figure 4 shows the cool flame extinction diameter as function of ambient pressure for both free-floated and fiber-supported droplets for pure n-dodecane burning in air. As mentioned earlier, as the pressure is increased above approximately 2 atm, reignitions were commonly observed, eventually leading to complete combustion of the fuel droplet. It is interesting to note that the 40 micron fiber shows relatively little effect on the extinction diameter. Figure 4. Cool flame extinction diameters as a function of ambient pressure for n-dodecane droplets burning in air. Since the cool flame extinction is an instability phenomenon where the dynamic balance between heat release and heat loss from the flame is lost at the lower turning point in the NTC region, one would expect addition of helium to have a substantial influence on the process. Figure 5 illustrates the effect of helium dilution on the extinction diameter for n-dodecane. Increase helium dilution leads to earlier cool flame extinction giving a larger extinction diameter.

Effect of helium dilution on cool flame extinction during n-dodecane droplet combustion. 5.4 Sooting behavior as function of ambient pressure: The effects and the process of soot formation during cool flame combustion remains largely unexplored. The shoot shell that forms during hot flame is stabilized by the balance of force between fluid mechanical drag and the thermophoretic force. At low pressures a stable spherical soot-shell is formed. However, as the pressure increase the soot-shell becomes diffuse and undefined. The reasons for this phenomenon is still not well understood. At low pressures, due to the low flame temperature of the cool flame, soot is not formed. The soot that is formed during the hot flame combustion is simply convected away from the droplet surface. But, when the pressure increases, residual soot is seen surrounding the droplet even after the hot flame extinction. The mechanisms behind this process has not been fully understood, and further analysis and research is needed.

The POD was notified and requested to ask Jeff to return the Fill Assembly into the field of view, which he did, confirming the observation. The DAFT Fill Assembly is a series of linear tubing connections with ‘appendages’ connected to it by tees. The foam that encase it (minicell) is in line with the thickness. investigation_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I
gravity_scope: Microgravity investigation; individual row gravity not separately encoded by source
text: The objectives of the SAFFIRE ( Spacecraft Fire Experiment ) experiments are to (1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test . The specific objective of SAFFIRE-I and SAFFIRE-II I tests is to determine how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low-gravity and whether it reaches a steady-state spread rate. The sample material for SAFFIRE-I and SAFFIRE-III is a composite fabric consisting of cotton on a fiberglass substrate (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight). It is called SIBAL cloth because it was developed for the Solid Inflammability Boundary at Low-Speeds (SIBAL) spaceflight experiment and has been used in many space experiments because it burns like cotton but maintains structural integrity after the cotton is consumed. SAFFIRE-I will be conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s while SAFFIRE-III will be run at a flow velocity of 30 cm/s . In addition to the 2 samples, data was also collected for pre-flow and post-flow. These image sets are denoted as F1 for pre-flow and F2 for post-flow. The experiment data is organized in PSI by sample number and camera number. There were 2 cameras capturing images during the experiment and they are denoted as C1 for camera 1 and C2 for camera 2. There are various documents and associated information located on the different tabs within the SAFFIRE Investigations records in PSI. A very useful document to review first is the “SAFFIRE Objectives, Development and Status.pdf” document
